title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
excerpt: A short guide to the little local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means, where it comes from and why linguists care that Rochdalians still use it.
summary: A short guide to the little local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means, where it comes from and why linguists care that Rochdalians still use it.
body:
Anyone from parts of Rochdale will recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” The small verb cruckle is used locally to mean rolling or twisting one’s ankle — the awkward, often walk‑offable misstep that still makes you wince. That everyday meaning is recorded in contemporary local projects and described by linguists working on Greater Manchester speech. (It’s not a medical term — cruckle simply names the action of turning your foot over.)

Why is it so strongly linked with Rochdale? Recent perceptual‑dialect research — the kind of work that asks hundreds of local people to mark and label accents and words on maps — shows that residents routinely associate particular words with particular boroughs. In a 2024 study of Greater Manchester folk‑linguistic labels, participants’ free comments listed “cruckle/cruckled” alongside other Rochdale items, which places the word in the borough’s visible local vocabulary. That kind of folk mapping is what gives a word social life: people hear it, use it and then point to it as a marker of place. (Researchers describe the method as a modified draw‑a‑map task, and they use GIS to show where labels cluster.)

Cruckle is not a recent invention. Historical dialect material shows an older verb crookle (also spelled in various ways) with senses such as “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble.” Those meanings sit in the same semantic field as the modern Rochdale use: bending or twisting, and the small repetitive‑action suffix ‑le is typical of many northern English dialect verbs. In short, cruckle looks like a local survival or variant of an older dialect verb family that originally meant “to make crooked” and later narrowed to the specific action of rolling an ankle in everyday Rochdale speech.

How exclusive is the word to Rochdale? Dialect researchers are cautious: administrative borders are poor predictors of where a word will or won’t be used. Perceptual studies and regional projects show that cruckle is highly salient in Rochdale (people there report and recognise it), and national and regional reports on Manchester‑area speech list “cruckled” under Rochdale. But similar or related forms (crookle, crukle) have been recorded historically elsewhere in northern and midland dialect glossaries. That means the form’s current social visibility is especially strong in Rochdale, even if related forms exist in historical records outside the borough.

Why should readers care? Tiny local verbs like cruckle are more than quaint curios. They are living traces of regional history, contact and sound change: the shape of the word (crook → crookle → cruck­le), the suffix pattern and the local social practice of using the word are all pieces of evidence linguists use to map how language marks identity. Projects that collect local voices — from university‑led “accent van” recordings to academic perceptual mapping — treat items like cruckle as precisely the sort of everyday data that shows how place and speech stay linked.

If you’ve got family examples, old spellings or a recording of someone saying the word, local archives and dialect projects welcome them. Contributions from speakers help researchers pin down where a word is used today and how its meaning has shifted over time. For now, the answer to “Why does Rochdale say cruckle?” is straightforward: people in Rochdale do say it, it names a recognisable action (rolling your ankle), it fits an old dialect pattern (crookle → cruckle), and perceptual dialect research shows the word is part of Rochdale’s local linguistic identity — even if identical forms turn up elsewhere in older records.

title: Tram Services Disrupted Between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre on Saturday
excerpt: No trams will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre until 2pm on Saturday, 5 September, due to improvement works. A bus replacement service will be in place for affected passengers.
content_html:
On Saturday, 5 September, tram services will be suspended between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre until 2pm due to scheduled improvement works on the Rochdale line. Passengers are advised that a bus replacement service will operate between the affected stops during this time.

Additionally, on Sunday, 6 September, from the start of service until 11am, there will be service changes across the network due to works at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar. Travellers should plan accordingly as these changes may affect their journeys.

For those using the Derker tram stop, the lift is currently out of service, and step-free access is available via a ramp from Cromford Street. Passengers heading towards Manchester can access the Manchester-bound platform directly, while those travelling towards Rochdale will need to use the track crossing.

Passengers requiring step-free access at the Failsworth tram stop should note that both lifts are out of service due to replacement works. They are advised to travel to Hollinwood to connect to services. For further assistance, customers can contact the Metrolink contact centre at 0161 244 1000, available from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends.

title: Rochdale Borough Council Set to Acquire Warwick Mill in Middleton
excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council is preparing to take ownership of Warwick Mill, with a major regeneration announcement for Middleton town centre expected on 7 September.
content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is understood to be preparing to take ownership of Warwick Mill, a significant step in the ongoing regeneration efforts for Middleton town centre. While the acquisition has not yet been formally confirmed, details are anticipated to be revealed at the 'Our Town, Our Future' event scheduled for Monday, 7 September.

The event will take place at Middleton Arena and is expected to include a major announcement regarding the regeneration of the town centre, alongside the results of a consultation involving nearly 2,500 residents and businesses. This consultation aims to gather local input on future developments and improvements.

In addition to the Warwick Mill announcement, the event will also highlight the first year of the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation. Key figures, including Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, co-chairs of the development corporation, will be in attendance, along with Rochdale Borough Council leader Councillor Neil Emmott and councillors June West and Dylan Williams.

The council was approached for comment regarding the acquisition but did not respond by the time of publication. Local residents and businesses are encouraged to attend the event to learn more about the future of Middleton town centre and the role Warwick Mill will play in its revitalisation.

Details regarding specific initiatives or projects resulting from this partnership have yet to be disclosed, but the club is optimistic about the positive impact it will have on its operations.

title: Man Arrested in Rochdale Town Centre While Wearing Balaclava
excerpt: A man was arrested by student police officers in Rochdale town centre after being spotted wearing a balaclava and acting suspiciously. He is wanted in connection with multiple alleged offences.
content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

15:47, 04 September 2026

A man was arrested by student police officers in Rochdale town centre after being spotted wearing a balaclava and acting suspiciously. He is wanted in connection with multiple alleged offences.

Student police officers on patrol in Rochdale town centre arrested a man wearing a balaclava who was acting suspiciously near the central bus station on Friday, 4 September 2026. The officers, part of Greater Manchester Police (GMP), conducted a stop search and recovered a bank card believed to be stolen.

Further investigations revealed that the man was wanted in connection with multiple alleged breaches of bail conditions. He was subsequently arrested on suspicion of theft and breach of bail offences and remains in police custody while enquiries continue.

Inspector Meena Yasin, of Rochdale North neighbourhood policing, stated that this arrest highlights their proactive commitment to maintaining safety in Rochdale town centre. She emphasised that anyone acting suspiciously can expect to be engaged by police officers during their patrols.

GMP Rochdale shared that their student officers are regularly patrolling the area to deter criminal activity and positively engage with the public, contributing to community safety.

title: New £12 Million Storage World Building Planned for Old Hall Street in Middleton
excerpt: Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd has submitted plans to Rochdale Council for a new mixed-use building on Old Hall Street, designed to reflect Middleton's mill heritage and replace a facility destroyed by fire.
content_html:
Self-Storage Performance Management International Ltd (SSPMI) has submitted a planning application to Rochdale Council for a new mixed-use building on Old Hall Street in Middleton. The proposed development, which is estimated to cost £12 million, aims to replace the previous Storage World facility that was destroyed by fire in June 2025.

The new building will feature a self-storage facility along with commercial units on the ground floor. Although it will occupy half the space of the former Storage World building, it will include two additional storeys to maintain the same storage capacity. The site previously housed the four-storey Albany Mill, constructed in 1884 and demolished in 1976, which was later replaced by a two-storey warehouse operated by Comfy Quilts until its relocation in 2006.

SSPMI acquired the site in 2013 and opened it as FlexiSpace in 2016, later rebranding it as Storage World. Following the fire, the company has been collaborating with Rochdale Development Agency and Middleton Mayoral Development Corporation to design a replacement that complements the ongoing regeneration efforts in the area.

The new Storage World building is intended to reflect Middleton's industrial heritage while also looking towards the future. The design aims to honour the site's historical significance while providing modern facilities for the community. The planning decision is expected to be made by Rochdale Council in the coming months.

title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real, water‑carved nook of rock that has gathered centuries of stories — but folklore and documentary record tell very different tales.
summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is a real, water‑carved nook of rock that has gathered centuries of stories — but folklore and documentary record tell very different tales.
body:
Walk under the stone viaduct at Healey Dell and you’ll find a narrow cleft where the River Spodden thunders through a rocky throat. Local signs and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre point visitors to a spot long called the Fairies’ Chapel — an evocative name that has attracted guidebooks, children’s trails and Victorian collectors of legend alike. The site is part of Healey Dell Nature Reserve, managed and promoted by Rochdale Borough Council as a place of industrial archaeology, woodland and waterfalls. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is indisputable: the place and its industrial history are real. The high stone viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II‑listed Victorian structure on the National Heritage List for England, and the valley contains the remains of mills, lodges and a former railway line now used as a trail. These are documented, protected features and form the historic backdrop that helped foreground the rock seat and grotto known as the Fairies’ Chapel. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

What created the ‘chapel’ is ordinary geology and the work of water. Guides and local interpretation explain that the Thrutch — a narrow gorge — contains a small natural excavation scored by the attrition of the river; older accounts and the Healey Dell visitor material say a great flood in early July 1838 altered or destroyed some of the rock formations formerly seen there. In short: the chapel‑like shapes are the result of erosion and historic landscape change, not built masonry. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

And the fairies? That is the realm of story. The best‑known accounts of the Fairies’ Chapel come from 19th‑century collectors such as John Roby, whose Traditions of Lancashire (first published in 1829 and reprinted in later nineteenth‑century editions) recorded a long narrative about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden, and encounters with fairy royalty in the Thrutch. Roby’s work, and later local retellings and guidebook extracts, mixed oral tradition, local gossip and romantic reconstruction — material to be enjoyed as folklore, not read as factual history. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Versions of the tale vary. In some tellings a Fairy King condemns witches to a rocky chapel; in others a prophecy or an enchanted hare leads a boastful miller into the fairy grotto. These stories have been printed and reworked for more than a century, and they fed Victorian visitors’ appetite for “haunted” beauty spots. The modern Healey Dell Heritage Centre preserves and retells many of these legends, and the valley’s trails now include family‑friendly interpretation such as a fairy grotto for children. Those activities keep the stories alive, but do not serve as evidence that supernatural beings live there. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean literal, sentient fairies as found in the stories — no contemporary, verifiable evidence supports that claim. If you mean “are there stories, traditions and a long local appetite for the uncanny” — absolutely. The Fairies’ Chapel is a genuine landscape feature with a documented industrial and geological history; it is also a cultural site where folklore collected since the early 19th century continues to be told and enjoyed. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

For visitors: treat the site as a meeting of nature, history and imagination. Respect the reserve’s paths and signage, enjoy the viaduct and waterfalls documented by Historic England and the borough, and bring a good torch if you try the narrow paths near the Thrutch. Above all, enjoy the stories as stories — valuable for what they tell us about local memory and the way places gather meaning over time. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

title: Horse in Rochdale left critically ill after being fed harmful food by campers
excerpt: A horse owner in Rochdale is seeking awareness after her horse, Frank, fell critically ill due to being fed harmful scraps by campers. The incident has raised concerns about the dangers of feeding horses human food.
content_html:
A horse in Rochdale has been left in a critical condition after being fed something dangerous by campers, according to his owner, Julie Kershaw. The incident occurred when Julie, 58, discovered her 13-year-old horse, Frank, trembling and unable to walk in the field where he is kept. Julie believes that the campers fed Frank human food, which led to his distress and subsequent health issues.

Julie was alerted to Frank's condition by her daughter, who was out walking with a friend when they found the horse shaking uncontrollably and struggling to breathe. They quickly issued a Facebook appeal to locate Julie, who rushed to the scene. Upon arrival, she found Frank in a dire state, fearing he would not survive the night. Julie stated, "He was really shaking and couldn't walk," highlighting the severity of the situation.

A vet was called and arrived within 40 minutes, administering four injections to treat Frank's condition, which was diagnosed as colitis, an infection in the colon. The emergency visit resulted in a vet bill of £235, with additional costs for food bringing the total to around £300. Julie expressed her frustration, stating, "It's just so scary - people don't realise how dangerous it is to feed horses."

This incident is not isolated; Julie noted that horse owners in the area have previously found harmful items such as chicken bones and vegetables discarded in fields. She urged the public to educate themselves on what is safe to feed horses, emphasising that even common treats can become dangerous if overfed. Julie's experience serves as a reminder of the potential risks associated with feeding horses human food.

title: Elite Hand Car Wash in Rochdale Fined for Minimum Wage Violations
excerpt: Elite Hand Car Wash on Molesworth Street has been penalised for failing to pay a worker the minimum wage, as part of a government initiative naming over 600 employers.
content_html:
Elite Hand Car Wash, located on Molesworth Street in Rochdale, has been penalised for failing to pay a worker the national minimum wage. The business, operated by Ms Misbah Khalil, is among 658 employers recently named by the government for similar violations.

The government initiative revealed that Elite Hand Car Wash owed £4,590.40 to one employee. This is part of a broader effort that has seen nearly £4 million returned to over 27,000 workers across the UK who were underpaid. Additionally, employers have faced penalties totalling £7 million for non-compliance with wage regulations.

The current national minimum wage is set at £12.71 per hour for workers aged 21 and over, £10.85 for those aged 18 to 20, and £8 for under-18s and apprentices. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds emphasised the importance of treating workers fairly, stating that responsible businesses understand that looking after their employees is essential for success.

As a result of this naming and shaming initiative, Elite Hand Car Wash may face increased scrutiny from both the public and regulatory bodies. Local residents and potential customers may wish to consider this information when choosing services in the area.

title: Boy, 13, stabbed in Rochdale town centre: six arrested, two bailed and stop-and-search powers extended
excerpt: Live story. Six teenage boys have now been arrested after a 13-year-old was stabbed in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night. Two have been released on bail, four remain in custody, and Section 60 stop-and-search powers in the town centre run until 3pm on Tuesday. Updated as Greater Manchester Police confirm developments.
content_html:
Latest, 08:30, Tuesday 1 September: six teenage boys have been arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 13-year-old boy in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night, 29 August. Two were arrested on Sunday and have since been released on bail. Four more were arrested on Monday and remain in custody. All six were held on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article, Greater Manchester Police said. The injured boy remains in hospital receiving treatment.

This is Rochdale Daily's single live story on the incident. It is updated in place, newest first, only when Greater Manchester Police or another primary source confirms a development. Earlier separate reports have been folded into this page; see the correction note at the foot.

What we know

The boy was stabbed during a serious assault in the town centre, near the Riverside shopping centre, on the evening of Saturday 29 August. Police described the incident as a serious assault alongside wider disorder in the town centre that night. He was taken to hospital, where he remains.

Monday 31 August: GMP confirmed four further arrests, all teenage boys, on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article. The two boys arrested on Sunday were released on bail while enquiries continue. Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said the force was continuing to make progress on the investigation and that violence on the streets would not be tolerated.

Monday 31 August: the Section 60 order covering Rochdale town centre was extended until 3pm on Tuesday 1 September. Under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, officers can stop and search people in the designated area without needing reasonable suspicion.

Sunday 30 August: GMP announced two arrests and put a 24-hour Section 60 order in place for the town centre from 3pm. Chief Inspector Michael Barton, neighbourhoods lead for GMP's Rochdale district, said detectives were reviewing CCTV, gathering witness statements and analysing intelligence to identify everyone involved.

Saturday 29 August: a 13-year-old boy was stabbed in the town centre. GMP log 2750 of 29/08/2026.

What we do not know

Police have not released the boy's condition beyond confirming he remains in hospital, and have not said what led to the assault. No one has been charged. Rochdale Daily will not name anyone arrested and will not publish speculation about motive or identity while the investigation is live.

How to help the investigation

Anyone who witnessed the incident, was in Rochdale town centre on Saturday evening, or has mobile phone, CCTV or dashcam footage is asked to contact GMP on 101, quoting log 2750 of 29/08/2026, or via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk. Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

title: One in seven Rochdale businesses could be overpaying business rates, research claims
excerpt: More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to BusinessRateChecker.com.
content_html:
More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to research from business rates intelligence company BusinessRateChecker.com.

The company's analysis examined 8,607 commercial properties in the borough and flagged 1,308 — 15.2% — as potentially over-assessed.

That was the highest proportion of any English local authority area included in BusinessRateChecker's analysis, ahead of Maidstone at 13.8%, Kirklees at 13.7% and Mid Suffolk at 13.7%.

BusinessRateChecker estimates the affected Rochdale properties could have grounds for reductions worth around £2.9 million collectively each year, equivalent to an average potential saving of approximately £2,217 for each property it identified.

However, the findings do not allege wrongdoing by Rochdale Borough Council.

The underlying rateable value of a commercial property is determined by the Valuation Office Agency. Councils then use the relevant rateable value and multiplier when calculating business rates bills.

Rupert Spiegelberg, CEO of BusinessRateChecker.com, told Rochdale Daily that businesses also have a responsibility to ensure the property information being used is accurate.

He said: “It is actually the responsibility of the property owner to update the VOA with changes in details of floor space, floor usage etc. Different RVs are applied to different spaces in a property. Many don't.”

He said larger companies were generally more likely to scrutinise their valuations because they had the resources to employ professional surveyors, while smaller businesses could be less likely to question what they were being charged.

He added: “Large businesses are usually quite up on this and will have the resources to hire surveyors to help them but for smaller businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops etc they tend not to question the bills as much.”

How Rochdale properties were assessed

BusinessRateChecker says its system compares the rate per square metre and zoning rates of individual properties with comparable nearby premises in the same category and valuation scheme.

It then examines factors including comparable rateable values and floor areas to identify properties whose valuations appear materially different from similar premises.

The company says tolerance bands are included to avoid flagging marginal cases.

Spiegelberg also told Rochdale Daily that the 1,308 figure could be an underestimate because some properties cannot be reliably assessed by its system.

Pubs are one example because valuations can depend partly on trading information which BusinessRateChecker does not have access to.

The company's own Rochdale dataset consequently records some properties as unassessable rather than assuming they are being charged correctly.

BusinessRateChecker currently analyses around 1.9 million commercial properties across England, using the published VOA rating list alongside other data to identify properties which may warrant further investigation.

Businesses can check their own property against comparable premises through the company's online checker.

title: REFORM UK DELIVERS: PEOPLE POWER BACKED BY REFORM SCRAPS DISASTROUS ROAD CLOSURES!
excerpt: Heywood Township councillors have voted unanimously to end the Hopwood Triangle traffic trial after sustained opposition from residents, while the Coronation Avenue HGV parking restriction will remain.
content_html:
Common sense has finally prevailed. At an extraordinary Heywood Township meeting last tonight, councillors voted UNANIMOUSLY to bring the Hopwood Triangle trial on Middleton Road and Magdala Street to an end and remove the road closures. The restriction preventing heavy wagons from parking on Coronation Avenue will remain in place, helping to protect local streets.

For residents, this decision has been a long time coming. The consultation results could hardly have been clearer: 86% of the approximately 700 respondents opposed the scheme. Yet despite that overwhelming response, the trial was approved and went ahead. Residents subsequently raised serious concerns about congestion, access, road safety and the effect on local businesses. People living on Manchester Road also felt they had been left out of the original consultation despite subsequently experiencing the impact of displaced traffic. The timing was another major concern. The trial began during the quieter summer holiday period, with residents warning that the true impact would become much more apparent once schools reopened and normal traffic levels returned. Last night, local people turned out in numbers to make sure their voices were heard. More than 50 residents attended the extraordinary meeting, but the size of the room at the old Police Station quickly became an issue. With residents understandably frustrated about access to a public meeting concerning their own streets, tensions rose and the meeting came close to being suspended. At that point, Reform UK Councillor Stuart Crawford intervened constructively. Recognising that many residents had already heard the Highways presentations and wanted councillors to make a decision, Stuart engaged directly with those in attendance, helped calm the situation and pressed for the meeting to move on to the vote rather than risk the evening ending without a decision. The vote was then taken. Every councillor voted to end the trial. That means the temporary road closures will now be removed, while the restriction on heavy wagons parking on Coronation Avenue will remain. And then there is the cost. The figures presented for the scheme are stark: £110,000 to install the temporary measures. That is £110,000 of public money associated with introducing and then removing a trial which had already been rejected by 86% of consultation respondents. The scheme was voted through back in November by Labour councillors Angela Brown, Paul O’Neil, Peter Hodgkinson, Peter Joinson, Susan Emmott and Liam O’Rourke, despite 86% of consultation respondents opposing it. Last night, the decision went the other way. Whatever political arguments follow, one fact should not be forgotten: local residents spoke up, kept speaking up and ultimately got the result they had been asking for. Reform UK will continue to stand with residents when decisions affecting their communities need to be challenged. A huge thank you to everybody who attended, everybody who responded to the original consultation, and everybody who refused to allow their concerns to be ignored. This was people power in action, and people power won.

title: From teaching assistant to PT: how Rochdale mum Jen Daker found the strongest version of herself
excerpt: After 16 years in education, mum-of-two Jen Daker has found a new calling as a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, combining 4am discipline, family life and a passion for helping others build confidence.
content_html:
There is an obvious physical transformation in Jen Daker’s story.

She is in the best shape of her life, trains with formidable discipline and has built a new career around fitness.

But Jen’s transformation goes far beyond how she looks.

For 16 years, Jen worked at the same school as a teaching assistant. She loved education, loved working with children and, for most of her adult working life, it was all she had known.

Then she became a mum.

After two pregnancies, her priorities began to change. Fitness, which had always been part of her life, became increasingly important not simply for how she looked, but for how she felt.

“I loved working in education, but after having children my priorities changed,” she said. “Fitness helped me so much physically and mentally after two pregnancies. I realised that if I could help other people feel like that, that was what I wanted to do.”

At 36, with two young children and a mortgage, changing careers was not the easy option.

Jen did it anyway.

Today she is a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, working with women and men of different ages, abilities and levels of confidence.

At the heart of her approach is one simple principle: consistency matters more than perfection.

Jen gets up at 4am to train.

There are mornings when staying in bed would be considerably easier, particularly after a broken night with the children.

But before school runs, clients, work and everything else involved in raising a family begins, Jen deliberately creates time that belongs to her.

“My workout isn’t just about keeping fit — it’s my time,” she said. “Before the school runs, work and everything else that comes with being a mum, I get an hour that’s just for me.”

Training first thing sets the tone for the rest of her day. She feels more energetic, her mood improves and she has already done something positive for herself before everybody else begins needing her.

It is an impressive level of discipline, but Jen is quick to point out that she does not wake every morning overflowing with motivation.

“Motivation comes and goes, but habits keep you going,” she said. “Some workouts are amazing and some aren’t. Showing up is what matters.”

That is also what she wants her clients to understand.

A healthy life is not built from one heroic gym session or one perfect week.

It is built from the ordinary things repeated often enough to matter. One walk. One healthier meal. One short workout. Then another.

Jen is equally clear that she did not make such a dramatic change alone.

Behind the early mornings, late evenings and weekend sessions is a family finding ways to make it work — and she credits her partner Damien as one of the central reasons she has been able to pursue it.

“I honestly couldn’t have made such a huge career change at 36, with two young children and a mortgage, without Damien,” she said.

“There are early mornings, late evenings and weekends where we’re juggling family life around work. Having someone who believes in you, encourages you and helps share the load makes such a difference.”

Her family, she says, have supported her from day one.

That strong relationship with Damien and her obvious love for her children sit at the centre of the life she has built rather than competing with it.

Jen does not pretend the balance is effortless. Some weeks work better than others.

“I’m still figuring it out,” she said. “I’ve learnt that looking after myself isn’t selfish — it’s necessary.”

Sometimes that means a workout. Sometimes a walk. Sometimes simply finding enough time for a quiet coffee.

For Jen, exercise has increasingly become about mental wellbeing.

She describes herself as having an active mind and says she can struggle to switch off. Exercise creates headspace.

“Life can feel hectic with work and children, and training gives me time to reset,” she said.

“It’s helped build my confidence and resilience. I don’t exercise because I want to look a certain way anymore. I do it because I know how much better I feel mentally when I move my body.”

But even someone capable of getting out of bed at 4am has had to learn that discipline is not the same thing as endlessly pushing harder.

There have been days when Jen has been exhausted or overwhelmed and recognised that another intense workout was not what her body needed.

Sometimes the healthier choice is a walk. Sometimes stretching. Sometimes rest.

“Listening to your body is just as important as pushing yourself,” she said. “Fitness should support your wellbeing, not become another source of pressure.”

She admits she is still learning to follow that advice herself.

Jen’s attitude towards food is similarly grounded in real life.

She loves food. Nothing is completely off limits.

And she does not want clients spending their lives bouncing between restrictive diets and guilt.

Her philosophy is that a healthy lifestyle must still leave room for birthdays, holidays, meals out and the foods people genuinely enjoy.

“One meal or one night out doesn’t undo months of healthy habits, just like one salad doesn’t suddenly make someone healthy,” she said.

“Food shouldn’t come with guilt.”

Instead, Jen encourages moderation and habits people can realistically sustain.

“Consistency wins every time. It’s what you do most of the time that matters, not what you do occasionally.

“Celebrate birthdays, enjoy holidays and make memories. Then just get back to your normal routine afterwards.”

There is no waiting for Monday. No declaring the month ruined because of one bad day.

“It’s never too late to start again,” Jen said. “Make your next choice a positive one and keep moving forward.”

Some of Jen’s proudest results cannot be measured with scales or photographed in a mirror.

One of her earliest clients found her after seeing a recommendation on Facebook. The pair had never met.

The woman had never even been inside a gym and arrived nervous and lacking confidence.

Over time, that changed. She began trusting herself. She became comfortable training. Eventually, while Jen was away on holiday, she went to the gym on her own — something she once would never have imagined doing.

“She is like a totally different person to the woman I met,” Jen said.

For Jen, that is the real reward.

“I’ve met people who were scared to walk into a gym become confident enough to train on their own,” she said.

“Most of the time the biggest transformation isn’t physical — it’s the confidence they gain in every part of their lives.”

She sees that particularly among mothers.

Motherhood can be all-consuming. Somewhere among school runs, work, washing, appointments and everybody else’s needs, women can begin feeling that the person they once were has disappeared.

Jen understands that. And she loves watching them find themselves again.

There is another misconception Jen would happily dismantle: that personal trainers are endlessly confident.

She believes the reality can be almost the opposite.

Working every day in an environment where bodies and physical performance are constantly visible can make trainers highly critical of themselves if they allow it.

And they certainly are not expecting new clients to arrive already fit.

“Most trainers just want to help people improve, whatever their starting point is,” she said.

Jen even experienced nerves herself after recently returning from a two-week holiday.

“I got the pre-gym nerves going back,” she said.

Her message to somebody frightened of walking into a gym for the first time is straightforward. Almost everybody has felt like that. Most other people are concentrating on their own workout, not watching yours.

“Every confident person in the gym was a beginner once,” Jen said. “The hardest part is walking through the door.”

There is perhaps no such thing as perfectly balancing motherhood, relationships, work, health, friendships and everything else expected of women.

Some days one thing will inevitably win.

But Jen Daker’s story suggests women can get remarkably close.

Today, Jen offers one-to-one personal training, small-group sessions and tailored online fitness plans, working with people of all ages and abilities.

She describes The Hybrid Hut as a gym where beginners, experienced athletes, younger people and older clients are all equally welcome.

Train with Jen Daker at The Hybrid Hut.

title: Oliver Coldman crowned champion golfer at Rochdale Golf Club Captain’s Final
excerpt: Oliver Coldman has won Rochdale Golf Club’s 2026 Captain’s Final with a two-round total of 133, four shots ahead of runner-up Steve Royle.
content_html:
Oliver Coldman has been crowned Rochdale Golf Club’s Champion Golfer for 2026 after winning the Captain’s Final during a weekend of competition at the club.

Coldman recorded rounds of 69 and 64 for a combined score of 133 to take the Captain’s Final title. Steve Royle finished runner-up after rounds of 67 and 70 gave him a total of 137.

The weekend also saw a series of other prizes decided. Raymond Clegg claimed Best Nett on Saturday, while Tom Wilson took Best Nett on Sunday.

Aaron Buckley won the Darren Ogden Memorial Trophy, awarded for nearest the pin in two on the 18th, with a distance of 2.13 metres. Steve George was named the lowest qualifier at 10 under par.

Rochdale Golf Club said the weekend had produced some brilliant golf despite the threat of rain, and congratulated all of the finalists and winners. The club also thanked the volunteers and staff involved in staging what it described as a special annual event.

A charity raffle was drawn during the weekend, with the club thanking supporters who bought tickets as well as the donors who supplied prizes. A full list of raffle prize winners is expected to be emailed to members over the coming days.

The Captain’s Final is one of the highlights of the club calendar, bringing together qualifiers for the concluding competition and recognising performances across the weekend.

title: Rochdale AFC installs 26 male sanitary bins to support fans after prostate cancer treatment
excerpt: Rochdale AFC has installed 26 specially designed male incontinence bins at the Crown Oil Arena and joined Prostate Cancer UK and phs Group's BOG STANDARD Charter through the Back in the Game campaign.
content_html:
Rochdale AFC has installed 26 specially designed sanitary bins in men's toilets at the Crown Oil Arena as part of a national drive to make live sport more accessible to men living with incontinence, including some who have undergone treatment for prostate cancer.

The club launched its involvement in the Back in the Game initiative at its home opener against Crawley Town, becoming the latest sporting organisation to sign up to the BOG STANDARD Charter run by Prostate Cancer UK and hygiene services provider phs Group.

Tobi Adebayo-Rowling helped launch the initiative ahead of the match alongside Dale director Richard Knight and Jez Williams of phs Group.

The campaign focuses on a practical problem which can prevent some men from returning to football grounds and other public venues after cancer treatment: finding a suitable place to dispose of male incontinence products discreetly and hygienically.

Rochdale AFC says specially designed bins have now been installed across its male toilets. The club has received Bronze accreditation under the BOG STANDARD Charter, which represents the installation of appropriate sanitary bins for men.

Silver accreditation also requires male incontinence products to be made available, while Gold adds a commitment to promoting awareness of prostate cancer and incontinence.

Richard Knight, who has personal experience of prostate cancer, said the club wanted supporters to feel able to return to the activities and social connections that matter to them following treatment.

He said: ‘Inclusion is important to us at the Club, and we didn’t ever want to think of any of our fans being unable to join.’

Mr Knight said seeing friends, spending time with family and attending matches can all form part of getting back into everyday life after treatment, and that the club wanted to remove a practical barrier for supporters.

WHY THE BINS MATTER

Urinary incontinence can affect men for a range of reasons and can occur following some treatments for prostate cancer. Men who use absorbent pads may need access to a sanitary bin large enough to dispose of them discreetly when away from home.

Prostate Cancer UK says prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in men in the UK. Its current risk information states that around one in eight men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime, rising to around one in four Black men.

The charity has argued that a lack of suitable disposal facilities in men's toilets can cause anxiety and embarrassment and, in some cases, discourage people from going out or returning to activities they previously enjoyed.

Nick Ridgman, Head of Support Services at Prostate Cancer UK, said the campaign is intended to make public venues more welcoming for men living with urinary incontinence and welcomed Rochdale AFC's decision to join.

The Back in the Game campaign specifically works with sports clubs because attending live sport can be an important part of people's social lives and routines. Campaign organisers said that, as of the Rochdale launch, 177 sports clubs across the UK had signed up to the BOG STANDARD, with 873 specially designed sanitary bins for men installed through the initiative.

Matthew Brabin, chief executive of phs Group, said some men can feel anxious about leaving home after prostate cancer treatment when they are uncertain whether suitable facilities will be available. He said the campaign aims to remove that barrier and help people resume normal social activities.

The wider Dispose with Dignity campaign, run by phs Group with Prostate Cancer UK since 2023, has called for better provision for men with incontinence in public toilets.

SUPPORT FOR MEN IN ROCHDALE

Anyone worried about their prostate cancer risk, going through treatment or living with its effects can contact Prostate Cancer UK's Specialist Nurses on 0800 074 8383. The charity also provides information and support through its website.

People with new or persistent urinary symptoms should seek medical advice. Urinary problems do not necessarily mean prostate cancer, but symptoms should be assessed appropriately rather than self-diagnosed.

Rochdale AFC's decision means supporters who need to dispose of male incontinence products can now do so in designated bins within the Crown Oil Arena's male toilets.

Further information about the Back in the Game campaign is available through phs Group, while prostate cancer information and support is available from Prostate Cancer UK.

title: Driver arrested after stolen vehicle recovered on Milnrow Road in Rochdale
excerpt: A driver has been arrested after Rochdale neighbourhood officers stopped a vehicle on Milnrow Road that police say had been reported stolen from North Wales.
content_html:
A driver has been arrested after Greater Manchester Police officers recovered a vehicle on Milnrow Road in Rochdale which police say had been reported stolen from North Wales.

According to Rochdale GMP, PC Maestro and PCSO Davies from the neighbourhood team sighted the vehicle on Milnrow Road during the afternoon of Saturday, August 15.

Police checks on the vehicle showed it had been recorded as stolen from North Wales.

The driver was arrested and the vehicle was seized by officers.

title: Wildfire emergency alert: an overreaction, or a sign of things to come?
excerpt: Millions of phones across England and Wales sounded a Government Emergency Alert as wildfire risk reached exceptional levels. Was the intrusive warning proportionate, or are Britons being introduced to a hazard we will increasingly have to live with?
content_html:
Millions of mobile phones across England and Wales emitted the unmistakable siren of the Government's Emergency Alerts system on Friday evening, carrying a warning about the risk of wildfires during exceptionally hot and dry conditions. People were urged not to light barbecues, campfires, bonfires or fireworks and to call 999 if they saw a fire.

For many people in Rochdale, where there was no wall of flame approaching their homes and no instruction to evacuate, the reaction was understandable: was this really what the country's most intrusive public-warning system was designed for? Emergency Alerts override ordinary phone settings and make a deliberately alarming noise intended to make people stop what they are doing immediately. Until recently, many people probably imagined receiving one only where there was a direct and imminent threat to life.

That makes the question worth asking. Was Friday's warning an overreaction, or was it an indication of how Britain's relationship with extreme weather is changing?

There is a reasonable argument that the Government must be careful not to overuse the system. Emergency warnings derive much of their effectiveness from their rarity. If people become accustomed to the siren being used for preventative advice that could have been distributed through television, radio, ordinary text messages and social media, warning fatigue becomes a real concern. A person who concludes that the alerts are unnecessarily dramatic may disable them and then miss a genuinely local warning about rapidly rising floodwater, an industrial accident or a fire approaching their home.

The Government should therefore be prepared to explain why this particular threshold was met and why an alert covering England and Wales was considered preferable to narrower regional warnings. Public confidence in an emergency system depends partly upon people understanding why its most intrusive warning mechanism has been activated.

However, dismissing the warning as hysteria would ignore the extraordinary situation confronting fire and rescue services this summer. Britain has experienced a succession of major wildfires during prolonged heat and drought. By Friday, national reporting indicated that the number of wildfires in England and Wales had already exceeded the 1,017 recorded during 2025, itself a record year. Dozens of fires were active around the country, major incidents had been declared, homes had been destroyed in the West Midlands and military personnel were being deployed to assist overstretched emergency services.

That changes the context considerably. Friday's message was not sent because somebody in Whitehall had suddenly discovered that dry grass can burn. It arrived during an active national wildfire emergency in which firefighters were already dealing with the consequences of repeated ignition in exceptionally dry landscapes.

The important distinction is between the probability of a fire starting and the severity of what may happen once one starts. Fire-danger measures do not necessarily predict that a particular patch of moorland will ignite. They indicate how easily vegetation may burn and how difficult a fire could become to control if ignition occurs. During ordinary British weather, carelessly discarded heat may produce a small scorched area. During prolonged heat, low humidity and very dry vegetation, the same ignition can develop into a fire requiring numerous appliances and many hours of firefighting.

Human behaviour therefore matters enormously. The Government cannot immediately cool the country, restore moisture to dried vegetation or remove weeks of accumulated heat from the landscape. It can, however, try to reduce avoidable sources of ignition. Disposable barbecues, bonfires, campfires, cigarettes, fireworks and other sources of heat can become much more consequential when the surrounding vegetation has effectively become fuel.

There is also a longer-term reason for taking the warning seriously. Britain is not becoming Spain, Greece or California overnight, and comparisons with those places can easily become exaggerated. Our climate, vegetation, housing patterns and emergency infrastructure are different. Nevertheless, the assumption that serious wildfire is an exotic problem belonging somewhere else is increasingly difficult to defend.

The UK has already experienced destructive moorland fires during previous hot summers, including the extensive Saddleworth Moor fires of 2018. For Rochdale this is not an abstract national concern. Moorland, grassland and countryside sit immediately beside settlements across the Pennine fringe, including areas around Littleborough, Wardle, Norden, Whitworth and the wider hills surrounding the borough. A serious moorland fire does not need to reach Rochdale town centre to affect Rochdale residents. Smoke, road closures, damaged habitats, exhausted emergency-service resources and threats to isolated properties can all spread consequences far beyond the flames themselves.

Climate science also points towards a future in which the weather conditions favourable to wildfire become more common. Research involving the Met Office and UK scientific institutions has concluded that human-caused climate change substantially increased the likelihood of the severe fire weather experienced during the 2022 heatwave. Climate-risk assessments anticipate more high fire-weather days as average temperatures rise, while longer periods of heat and drought can leave vegetation increasingly vulnerable to ignition.

That does not mean climate change can be blamed automatically for every individual fire. Fires still require ignition, fuel and conditions that allow them to spread. Land management, deliberate arson, accidental ignition and the speed of the emergency response all remain important. But the broader direction is difficult to ignore: a warmer climate can create more frequent periods in which an otherwise minor act of carelessness has much larger consequences.

This is why there is a sensible position between panic and dismissal. The Government should not turn the Emergency Alerts system into an electronic public-information poster. If the siren sounds too often for advice that is not genuinely urgent, its effectiveness may be weakened. Equally, a warning designed to prevent new fires during an already exceptional national wildfire situation is not obviously frivolous simply because no flames were visible from the recipient's window.

In fact, prevention may be one of the strongest arguments for using the system. Waiting until a wildfire is already moving towards houses means waiting until much of the opportunity to stop the emergency has disappeared. If a short national warning prevents even a small number of avoidable ignitions at a time when firefighters are already stretched, the intervention may prove proportionate despite its dramatic presentation.

The most interesting aspect of Friday's alert is therefore not the ten seconds of noise. It is what the noise was about. Britain has spent generations regarding wildfire principally as a rural inconvenience or an overseas catastrophe. Emergency planners are now treating it as a hazard capable of threatening homes, infrastructure and life on a sufficiently large scale to justify use of a national warning system.

For residents of Rochdale and the wider Pennine area, that deserves attention. Our landscape contains precisely the combination of moorland, grass, woodland and settlements that can make prolonged dry conditions problematic. The lesson is not that every warm weekend should cause millions of phones to scream. It is that the range of emergencies Britain prepares for may be changing.

If wetter summers return and warnings of this kind remain extremely rare, Friday's alert may ultimately be remembered as an unusually cautious intervention during an exceptional season. If periods of intense heat, drought and severe fire weather become more frequent, it may instead look like an early example of something the public later comes to regard as normal.

That is the uncomfortable possibility behind the alarm. The argument is not really about whether people were irritated by their phones. It is about whether Britain is entering a period in which hazards once considered unusual have to become part of ordinary civil protection.

Whether Friday's alert was perfectly calibrated is open to debate. The underlying wildfire risk is not.

title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.

title: Rochdale businesses urged to back Denehurst House in £30-a-month veterans challenge
excerpt: A Rochdale veterans support organisation is asking 100 local businesses to pledge £30 a month to help keep Denehurst House operational and support former service personnel in need.
content_html:
A Rochdale veterans support organisation has launched a drive to recruit 100 local businesses willing to pledge £30 a month towards keeping Denehurst House operational.

Get Together After Serving CIC, which is behind the campaign, says Denehurst House provides support for veterans including emergency housing, hot meals and mental health support. The organisation is promoting the appeal as the Rochdale 100 Businesses Challenge and is asking firms across the borough to make a regular monthly contribution.

If all 100 places are filled, the campaign would generate £3,000 each month in pledged support, equivalent to £36,000 over a full year if every business remained involved for 12 months. The appeal describes the contribution as a relatively small commitment for an individual business which, collectively, could make a significant difference to the service.

Campaign material highlights community spirit, warm meals and local businesses working together, with the message: 'Together, we keep Denehurst House operational.' It also says the project aims to provide a lifeline to veterans when they need it most.

The initiative is seeking support from companies of all sizes rather than relying on a handful of major donors. That model would spread the cost across the local business community while giving Denehurst House a more predictable stream of recurring income.

Local businesses interested in joining the challenge are being asked to contact Get Together After Serving CIC by emailing hello@gtascic.co.uk.

Rochdale Daily is publishing the appeal as today's front-page community story to help local firms understand what is being requested, how the funding model works and how they can take part.

title: Rochdale businesses urged to back Denehurst House in £30-a-month veterans challenge
excerpt: Get Together After Serving CIC is calling on 100 local businesses to pledge £30 a month to help keep Denehurst House operational and support veterans in need.
content_html:
A Rochdale veterans organisation has launched a drive to recruit 100 local businesses willing to contribute £30 a month towards the running of Denehurst House.

Get Together After Serving CIC, known as GTAS CIC, is promoting the Rochdale 100-Businesses Challenge as a way for firms across the borough to make a relatively small regular contribution which, collectively, could provide significant ongoing support.

Campaign material shared with Rochdale Daily says Denehurst House provides support for veterans including emergency housing, hot meals, company and mental-health support. The organisation describes the building as a lifeline for former service personnel at times when they may be facing isolation, housing difficulties or other pressures.

The campaign is asking for 100 businesses to pledge £30 each month. If all 100 places are filled, that would amount to £3,000 a month in regular support for the project, or £36,000 over a full year if every pledge remained in place.

GTAS CIC says the purpose of the challenge is not simply to raise money, but to create a lasting partnership between local employers, traders and the veterans community. Its campaign artwork highlights volunteering, shared meals and local business involvement under the message that stronger community links can create a real impact.

Denehurst House is presented by the organisation as a base where veterans can find practical help as well as human contact. For businesses, the proposition is deliberately simple: £30 a month, with the combined backing of 100 companies intended to provide a more predictable stream of funding than one-off donations alone. title: Rochdale AFC Netball launched as Rochdale Netball Club joins Dale family
excerpt: Rochdale Netball Club is becoming Rochdale AFC Netball in a new partnership with Rochdale AFC and its Community Trust, bringing nearly 200 weekly players into the club's wider sporting family.
content_html:
Rochdale Netball Club is joining the Rochdale AFC family under a new identity as Rochdale AFC Netball, in a partnership designed to grow the sport and create more opportunities for women, girls and the wider community across the borough.

The agreement brings together Rochdale AFC, Rochdale AFC Community Trust and one of the borough's established community sports clubs under the wider 'Our Teams' banner.

Rochdale Netball Club currently runs teams from under-six level through to seniors, with nearly 200 players taking to the court each week. Under the new Rochdale AFC Netball identity, the organisations hope to strengthen the route from school participation into junior and adult club netball while also expanding opportunities in coaching, volunteering and leadership.

The partnership is expected to support new programmes in schools, holiday provision, health and wellbeing and volunteer development. The shared Rochdale AFC identity could also open up additional opportunities for sponsorship, commercial support, community events and promotion through the football club.

Amy Williams, Chair of Rochdale AFC Netball, described the move as a fantastic opportunity for both the club and the sport locally, saying joining the Rochdale AFC family would provide a stronger platform to grow the game and inspire more women and girls to become involved.

Rochdale AFC chief executive Laura Thomas, herself a former netball player, said she was thrilled to welcome the club into the wider Rochdale AFC family and stressed that the club's ambition to build a thriving community extends beyond football.

Ryan Bradley, Community Director at Rochdale AFC Community Trust, said the football club, charity and netball club shared common values and could combine their respective strengths. He said bringing the organisations together under one brand would raise netball's profile in Rochdale and strengthen support for volunteers, coaches, community outreach and school work.

Rochdale AFC Netball will be based at Edgar Wood. The Community Trust also pointed to plans for the Community Football and Wellbeing Hub at Bowlee, saying the geographical proximity of the projects made closer cooperation a natural step.

The move follows a wider trend in British sport in which professional football and rugby clubs have partnered with netball organisations to increase visibility, participation and long-term sustainability. In Rochdale, the organisations say their approach will remain community focused and open to people of all ages.

Further information about Rochdale AFC Netball teams, programmes and opportunities to get involved is expected to be announced in due course.

title: LIVE: Murder ruled out as investigation continues into death of Nathan Haigh in Rochdale
excerpt: Greater Manchester Police has ruled out murder as a line of enquiry into the death of 31-year-old Nathan Haigh at Great Howarth, while enquiries into the circumstances continue.
content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

00:56, 21 August 2026 — Greater Manchester Police has ruled out murder as a line of enquiry into the death of 31-year-old Nathan Haigh at Great Howarth in Rochdale. Police say the investigation into the circumstances of his sudden death remains ongoing while the full results of the post-mortem examination are awaited.

The 37-year-old woman who was originally arrested on suspicion of murder has been released on bail in relation to an assault investigation. An arrest or release on bail is not a finding of guilt, and no inference of guilt should be drawn.

Detective Inspector Georgina Fearn, of Rochdale CID, said specialist officers continue to support Nathan's family. Police said their enquiries had established that murder was no longer being treated as a line of enquiry and reiterated that they do not believe there is a wider risk to the public.

Nathan Haigh, 31, was found unresponsive inside an address on Great Howarth after emergency services were called at around 7.39pm on Tuesday 11 August. CPR was commenced, but he was pronounced dead shortly afterwards.

Police initially described the circumstances as suspicious and arrested a 37-year-old woman on suspicion of murder while several lines of enquiry were explored. The subsequent decision to rule out murder represents a substantive change in the status of the investigation.

Rochdale Daily will continue to update this live report when further verified information is released by Greater Manchester Police or other authoritative sources.

title: A-Level results day: Rochdale students discover what comes next
excerpt: Students across Rochdale are receiving their A-Level results today, as the town's sixth form record comes under the spotlight and Rochdale MP Paul Waugh begins his new role at the Department for Education.
content_html:
Students across Rochdale have been opening their A-Level results today, bringing two years of study, examinations and anxious waiting to an end as young people discover whether they have secured university places, apprenticeships or their next step into employment.

Results day on Thursday 13 August comes during another strong year nationally. Across the UK, 28.5% of A-Level entries were awarded an A* or A, while in England the figure was 28.3%. More than 262,000 UK 18-year-olds had been accepted onto university courses by results day.

In the North West, 26.5% of A-Level entries received an A* or A in 2026, compared with 26.6% in 2025 and 23.5% in 2019. The figures continue to show a substantial regional divide, with London recording 32.7% of entries at A* or A this year.

For Rochdale, particular attention falls on Rochdale Sixth Form College, which has developed a strong academic record since opening in September 2010. The college was created following longstanding concerns about post-16 attainment in the borough and the number of local students travelling outside Rochdale for sixth-form education.

The college's early results quickly attracted national attention. It was ranked second among sixth form colleges for value added in Department for Education performance tables in 2013 and later achieved first place for A-Level progress for several consecutive years. By January 2019 it had been ranked first in Department for Education performance tables for five years running, and in 2021 it won Sixth Form College of the Year at the Tes FE Awards.

More recent government performance data has continued to show strong progress. Department for Education figures for 2024 recorded an average A-Level result of B- at Rochdale Sixth Form College and an A-Level progress score of +0.41, classified as well above average. The 2025 figures again recorded an average result of B-, with an average point score of 37.33 and a progress measure of +0.48, also classified as well above average.

The historical picture matters because Rochdale Sixth Form College was established in part to tackle a period in which the borough's A-Level performance had lagged behind national averages. Its subsequent performance provides a significant contrast with the concerns that led to the college being established more than 15 years ago.

Today's results are also notable politically because Rochdale's MP, Paul Waugh, has recently joined the Department for Education. Mr Waugh was appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education in July 2026, giving Rochdale a direct connection to national education policy.

Today's A-Level cohort completed almost all of its education before Mr Waugh entered the department, so the 2026 results cannot reasonably be attributed to his tenure. Future results, however, will increasingly provide part of the national record against which the Government's education policies — and the ministers responsible for them — are judged.

That will be particularly relevant in areas such as Rochdale because regional inequality remains one of the clearest challenges facing education ministers. This year's figures show 32.7% of A-Level entries in London receiving A* or A, compared with 26.5% in the North West and 23.1% in both the North East and East Midlands.

For students receiving their results today, however, national statistics and ministerial records are unlikely to be the immediate priority. For some, the results will confirm university places they have worked towards for years. Others will move into apprenticeships, employment or further study, while students who have missed required grades can consider Clearing and alternative routes.

Whatever the individual results, today marks the end of one chapter for Rochdale's students and the beginning of another.
