title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

title: Are Facebook Groups Becoming the Gatekeepers of Local News?
excerpt: Large community Facebook groups now play a major role in determining which local stories residents see, raising questions about moderation, access to information and the influence of digital gatekeepers.
content_html:
Recent posts from independent local news publishers have, at times, remained pending approval or failed to appear in large community Facebook groups. The reasons are not always clear and may range from routine moderation and administrative delays to editorial decisions made by group administrators.

Whatever the explanation, the situation raises a wider question about how much influence large local Facebook groups have over the news and viewpoints residents are exposed to.

Many of these groups have memberships larger than the circulation of traditional local newspapers. For thousands of people, they have become the primary place where local news, events and community discussion are discovered. Decisions about which posts are approved can therefore have a significant impact on what information reaches the public.

Independent journalism exists to report what is happening within a community, regardless of whether those stories are politically convenient or uncomfortable. It should not matter whether a story reflects positively or negatively on any political party, campaign group or public body. The role of journalism is to inform readers, not to tell them what to think.

Equally, moderation is an important part of running any online community. Administrators are entitled to remove unlawful material, spam, abuse, hate speech or defamatory content. However, where lawful reporting is prevented from reaching large community audiences, it is reasonable to ask whether local people are receiving a balanced picture of events.

Too often, debate can become centred on labels rather than evidence. Terms such as 'misinformation', 'divisive' or 'harmful' should only be used where they can be supported by facts. If reporting is inaccurate, it should be corrected. If facts are disputed, they should be challenged with evidence. Robust debate is healthier than silent suppression.

Independent local journalism has become increasingly important as traditional local newsrooms have shrunk. Smaller publishers often report stories that might otherwise receive little attention, giving residents access to a broader range of information and perspectives.

Ultimately, Facebook groups have become powerful gatekeepers of local information. That influence brings responsibility. While moderators are free to manage their communities as they see fit, readers should also recognise that what appears in a Facebook feed is not necessarily the full picture of what is happening across Rochdale borough.

A healthy democracy depends on people having access to a range of lawful reporting and being trusted to reach their own conclusions.

title: Rochdale's biggest event returns this Saturday as Feel Good Festival takes over the town centre
excerpt: Thousands of people are expected to descend on Rochdale town centre this Saturday as the borough's biggest annual event returns with headline performances from Gabrielle, Ash and Starsailor alongside a packed programme of live music, street food and family entertainment.
content_html:
Rochdale's biggest and most attended annual event returns on Saturday 8 August as the Feel Good Festival once again transforms the town centre into one of Greater Manchester's largest free celebrations of live music, food and entertainment.

Thousands of visitors are expected to flock to Rochdale throughout the day, with the stunning backdrop of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall providing the setting for a packed programme of performances, street food and family activities.

Headlining this year's main stage in Town Hall Square is BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, whose career has produced chart-topping hits including Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She will be joined by legendary Northern Irish rock band Ash and indie favourites Starsailor, alongside performances from The Allergies, Alex Spencer, K-STATE, Metro and Dave Sweetmore.

Away from the main stage, live music will continue throughout the day inside venues across Rochdale town centre, with pubs, bars and independent venues hosting local artists and emerging talent, creating a festival atmosphere across the borough.

The festival officially opens at 11:30am, with entertainment continuing throughout the afternoon and evening before the headline performances conclude at approximately 10:45pm.

One of the festival's biggest attractions remains its popular Food and Drink Village, where visitors can enjoy everything from gourmet burgers and pizzas to international street food, loaded fries, desserts, artisan coffee, ice cream, licensed bars and locally produced drinks. Independent traders from across the region will once again showcase a wide variety of food and beverages throughout the day.

Visitors travelling by car are encouraged to use Rochdale town centre's public car parks, including those at Number One Riverside, Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre and nearby council-operated facilities. Due to the popularity of the event and temporary road closures, organisers recommend arriving early or making use of public transport wherever possible. Rochdale Railway Station, Rochdale Interchange and the Bee Network Metrolink stop are all within a short walking distance of the festival site.

The event has been designed to be accessible for everyone. Step-free routes are available throughout the main festival site, accessible toilets are provided, designated accessible viewing areas will be available near the main stage and British Sign Language interpretation will accompany selected performances. Festival stewards will also be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors requiring additional support.

Since launching in 2008, the Feel Good Festival has welcomed internationally renowned artists to Rochdale and has become one of the North West's premier town-centre music festivals. Beyond the entertainment, it provides a significant boost to the local economy, with restaurants, cafés, bars, shops and hotels all benefiting from the influx of visitors.

Whether you're heading into town to sing along with Gabrielle, relive the guitar anthems of Ash, enjoy Starsailor's iconic hits or simply spend the day sampling fantastic food while supporting local businesses, the Feel Good Festival promises another unforgettable celebration of everything Rochdale has to offer.

title: Interactive Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival heading to Castleton this autumn
excerpt: Families looking for an autumn day out won't have far to travel as The Patchworks Interactive Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival returns to nearby Castleton with pumpkin picking, games, food and seasonal entertainment.
content_html:
Autumn is just around the corner and one of the Peak District's newest family attractions is preparing to welcome visitors from across Greater Manchester.

The Patchworks Interactive Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival will return to Castleton throughout October, offering a traditional pumpkin-picking experience alongside interactive games, seasonal activities, marshmallow toasting, food, drinks and plenty of opportunities for those all-important autumn photographs. The attraction is expected to operate across selected dates from early October until Halloween.

Located at the foot of Winnats Pass near Castleton, the attraction is less than an hour's drive from Rochdale, making it an ideal day trip for families during weekends and the October half-term holidays.

Visitors will be able to choose their own pumpkins directly from the patch before enjoying a range of family-friendly activities designed for children and adults alike. Organisers are also promising refreshments, hot drinks, sweet treats and seasonal food throughout the event. Advance online booking is available and is recommended for the busiest dates.

Pumpkin patches have become one of Britain's fastest-growing seasonal attractions, offering an alternative to traditional Halloween events while encouraging families to spend time outdoors together. Combined with the spectacular scenery surrounding Castleton and Winnats Pass, organisers are hoping visitors will enjoy a full day out in the Peak District.

For many Rochdale families, destinations such as Castleton have become popular autumn escapes thanks to their close proximity and beautiful countryside setting. The combination of pumpkin picking, interactive entertainment and locally prepared food makes The Patchworks another welcome addition to the region's growing calendar of family-friendly seasonal events.

The event is expected to conclude at the end of October, with Halloween marking the final days of this year's Pumpkin Patch and Autumn Festival.

title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club in Heywood, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend a weekly Armed Forces Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at The Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Armed Forces Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10am at The Flying Horse Hotel, Heywood.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Heywood Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

title: Fresh complaints over persistent landfill odour as Heywood residents report 'sewer' stench and fly infestation
excerpt: Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong foul odour and increasing numbers of flies, prompting renewed questions over the long-running issues surrounding the Pilsworth South landfill site.
content_html:
Residents across Heywood have once again reported a strong unpleasant smell drifting across parts of the town, with many describing an odour resembling sewage, rotting waste or landfill gas. The latest complaints have reignited concerns over the long-running issues surrounding the nearby Pilsworth South landfill site.

Several residents also reported unusually high numbers of flies, a problem which campaigners have previously associated with the landfill during earlier periods of odour complaints.

Rebecca Hodkinson wrote: "Yep... Unfortunately. And the amount of flies is something else this year."

Billy Casper added: "It stunk rotten like sewers when I was walking up Heywood past Iceland at 5.30 this evening. I don't think it was the landfill though."

Jeanette Noble commented: "I've been smelling it on Darnhill for a few months and the amount of flies is terrible."

Although some residents believe the smell may have originated elsewhere, the recurrence of similar complaints has led many to question whether problems linked to the landfill have returned.

The issue first gained widespread public attention during 2024 when thousands of complaints were submitted to the Environment Agency by residents across Heywood, Middleton, Bury and Rochdale. The smell became one of the borough's most significant environmental concerns, leading to regulatory investigations into landfill gas management and odour control measures at the site.

Under environmental law, landfill sites are permitted to operate only under an Environmental Permit issued by the Environment Agency. Operators are legally required to use Best Available Techniques (BAT) to prevent or minimise pollution, including offensive odours. Persistent smells escaping beyond the site boundary are not automatically unlawful, but they can lead to regulatory enforcement where permit conditions are breached. The Environment Agency has powers to require operational improvements, vary permit conditions, or take enforcement action where appropriate.

The issue has also attracted political attention. West Heywood councillor Angela Brown has repeatedly encouraged residents to report every odour incident directly to the Environment Agency, stressing that detailed reports help investigators establish patterns and build evidence. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has likewise raised concerns publicly and in Parliament regarding the impact of the landfill on surrounding communities.

Controversy has continued following approval for further landfill operations despite ongoing complaints from nearby residents. Campaigners argue that expansion should not proceed until odour problems have been fully resolved, while regulators maintain that environmental permits require operators to comply with strict controls.

Residents experiencing offensive odours are encouraged to report incidents directly to the Environment Agency, recording the date, time, location, weather conditions and a description of the smell. Multiple reports from different locations can assist investigators in determining whether a wider environmental incident is occurring.

For many residents, the recurring nature of the complaints is becoming increasingly frustrating. While only a full investigation can determine the source of any individual odour event, the persistence of reports over recent years demonstrates that confidence among the local community has yet to be restored.

title: Late-night fireworks return to Shawclough and Healey as residents' frustration grows
excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey have reported a second consecutive evening of fireworks after 11pm, with growing frustration over disrupted sleep, distressed pets and concerns for wildlife near Healey Dell Nature Reserve.
content_html:
Residents across Shawclough and Healey have once again reported being disturbed by late-night fireworks, with explosions heard at approximately 11.21pm on Sunday evening. The latest incident marks the second consecutive night of reports, leaving many residents questioning when meaningful action will be taken to tackle the ongoing nuisance.

For many households, the issue extends far beyond a brief display. Parents have described children being woken after bedtime, pet owners report anxious and distressed animals, and residents working early shifts say repeated interruptions to their sleep are becoming increasingly difficult to tolerate.

The repeated use of fireworks late at night has also prompted renewed concerns for local wildlife. Healey Dell Nature Reserve, together with the surrounding woodland, provides important habitat for nesting birds, bats and other protected species. Wildlife organisations have long warned that unexpected loud explosions can disturb feeding, nesting and breeding behaviour, particularly during sensitive periods of the year.

Residents have increasingly questioned whether existing legislation is sufficient to prevent repeated anti-social use of fireworks. While fireworks can be legally purchased and used subject to restrictions, businesses selling them must comply with licensing and storage regulations. However, any decision to suspend or revoke a retailer's licence would require evidence that they had breached those legal requirements. Simply because fireworks are being misused by individuals does not automatically mean a retailer has acted unlawfully.

Enforcement remains difficult, particularly when fireworks are discharged from private property under the cover of darkness. Identifying those responsible often relies on witness evidence, CCTV or reports made at the time of the incident.

Nevertheless, residents say patience is wearing thin. After another evening of disrupted sleep, many are calling for stronger enforcement, tighter controls on sales and greater action against those repeatedly using fireworks in residential neighbourhoods late at night.

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural and community celebrations when used responsibly. However, repeated displays after 11pm in quiet residential areas are a very different matter. Communities should not have to endure nightly disruption, frightened pets, exhausted children and unnecessary disturbance to local wildlife. As complaints continue to mount, many residents are asking a simple question: when will enough finally be enough?

title: Reform UK councillors reject proposed allowance increase
excerpt: The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.
content_html:
The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.

The controversial increase was rubber-stamped by Labour councillors present at the full council meeting on Thursday 16 July, with every single Labour member in attendance voting in favour. In contrast, Reform UK councillors voted unanimously against the motion, while other political groups on the council either abstained or voted against. At a time when local residents continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures and squeezed household budgets, the Reform UK group believes it is entirely wrong to increase politician payouts funded by the taxpayer. Each Reform UK councillor has now individually written to council officers to officially opt out of the increase, ensuring the extra funds remain in the public purse.

Speaking on behalf of the Reform UK group, Group Leader Councillor John Taylor said: "Hard-working families across Rochdale are having to make tough financial decisions every single day. The idea that local politicians should push through an increase in their own allowances—as Labour did at the full council meeting on 16 July—is completely out of touch with reality. We were elected to serve our community, not to line our own pockets. Reform UK voted against this increase in the chamber, and every single member of our group has now formally instructed council governance that we will refuse to take a single extra penny. We urge councillors from other parties to do the right thing and follow our lead." Reform UK remains committed to promoting financial responsibility, cutting waste in local government, and ensuring council resources are spent directly on frontline public services for the people of Rochdale.

title: Low-flying helicopter heard across Rochdale as residents ask what happened
excerpt: Residents across Rochdale reported hearing and seeing a helicopter flying unusually low over the borough on Monday evening, prompting widespread discussion on local social media.
content_html:
A low-flying helicopter was heard and seen across several parts of Rochdale on Monday evening, with many residents taking to local social media groups to ask why the aircraft was circling over the borough.

Reports came from multiple neighbourhoods, with people describing the helicopter as flying lower than usual and remaining in the area for an extended period. The activity quickly prompted speculation online, with some residents wondering whether a major incident had taken place.

At the time of publication, neither Greater Manchester Police nor the National Police Air Service had announced a major incident linked to the helicopter, and no public statement had been issued explaining its deployment.

Police helicopters are routinely used to support officers on the ground across Greater Manchester. They may assist with searching for missing people, tracking suspects, providing aerial observations during ongoing incidents or supporting other emergency service operations. Not every deployment results in a public announcement, particularly where there is no wider risk to the public or where operational reasons prevent police from releasing information.

It is therefore not unusual for residents to notice the aircraft without an immediate explanation being made available.

Anyone who witnessed an emergency incident connected with the helicopter or has information that could assist police should contact Greater Manchester Police through the appropriate reporting channels. If there is an immediate threat to life or crime in progress, people should always dial 999.

Rochdale Daily will update this article if Greater Manchester Police or the National Police Air Service releases further information about Monday evening's deployment.

title: Is this how the NHS treats its own? 81-year-old man left outside Rochdale Infirmary for ten hours
excerpt: An 81-year-old man spent around ten hours lying outside Rochdale Infirmary while members of the public repeatedly sought help. Rochdale Daily investigates what happened and asks who held responsibility for his care.
content_html:
An 81-year-old man lay confused, incoherent and unable to stand outside the grounds of Rochdale Infirmary for around ten hours while members of the public desperately tried to persuade the emergency services, hospital staff and social care agencies to help him.

The disturbing incident was witnessed and filmed by the editor of Rochdale Daily, who saw passers-by provide the man with water, blankets, cushions, food and cardboard while repeated attempts were made to establish which public service had responsibility for his welfare.

The man was found lying on the ground near the hospital car park. He appeared unable to stand unaided and could rarely string together more than two words. He later told those attempting to assist him that he was 81 years old.

Security staff were monitoring the situation and informed members of the public they had contacted Greater Manchester Police. Officers did not arrive until approximately ten hours after the ordeal began.

Members of the public repeatedly attempted to request an ambulance. During those calls, callers say they were informed the man was barred from the ambulance service because of previous behaviour and because of other matters that could not be discussed due to data protection legislation.

The precise legal status of any restriction involving the man has not yet been independently confirmed. However, Rochdale Daily holds video footage of the day's events, including numerous conversations between witnesses, members of the public and staff.

Whatever may have happened previously, the man lying on the ground that day appeared incapable of posing any immediate threat. He was confused, unable to stand, largely unable to communicate and repeatedly soiled himself while lying outside the hospital.

Members of the public also attempted to contact Rochdale Council Adult Social Care, people believed to be relatives, homelessness organisations and local charities. Appeals were placed on Facebook asking whether anyone knew the gentleman or could help locate family members.

Some comments on social media suggested the man had brought the situation upon himself if he had previously abused NHS staff. One commenter wrote: "You don't get barred from the NHS for nothing."

No one should minimise the abuse suffered by NHS workers. Nurses, doctors, paramedics, receptionists and security staff face unacceptable levels of violence, intimidation and verbal abuse every day. Staff deserve protection, and where individuals genuinely pose a danger, organisations are entitled to implement appropriate safeguards.

But that was not the man witnessed by Rochdale Daily.

For hour after hour he remained lying on the ground, unable to stand, struggling to communicate and apparently incapable of caring for himself. Members of the public did not witness any aggression towards staff, security or those trying to help him.

Throughout the day, ambulance vehicles entered and left the hospital site. Witnesses attempted to flag them down, but the vehicles continued past. Others reportedly stopped only to explain they were unable to assist.

Approximately six hours into the incident, two nurses accompanied by hospital security entered the car park and spoke with those attempting to help the man.

According to the editor's contemporaneous video recording, the nurses stated they could not treat the gentleman unless the situation became a matter of "life or death".

When asked what 'life or death' would look like to an untrained member of the public, they replied: "We couldn't tell you."

Members of the public then asked whose duty of care the gentleman fell under if he died while no organisation would intervene. One member of staff replied: "Not you."

When pressed as to which organisation would carry responsibility if treatment continued to be refused, those present say no clear answer was given.

One nurse then stated that the gentleman's breathing would have to stop before intervention could take place.

The editor replied that she could not see him breathing. The nurse looked over the wall towards the gentleman and responded that his chest was rising and therefore he was breathing.

During the exchange, one nurse was recorded saying: "This is what you get when you're on it day and night."

When asked what she meant by the remark, no explanation was given.

Later in the incident, a person identifying themselves as a family member stated the gentleman had dementia. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that relationship or medical diagnosis.

A representative from Get Together After Serving CIC attended the scene after becoming aware of the incident and also attempted to secure medical assistance.

The representative said they were informed the gentleman was subject to a restraining order involving the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust and that members of the public would need to transport him outside the area before treatment could be sought elsewhere.

Rochdale Daily has requested clarification from the Trust regarding that alleged restriction.

Throughout the ordeal, members of the public continued caring for the gentleman. Bottles of water, blankets, cushions, cardboard and food were brought to make him more comfortable while people searched desperately for someone willing to take responsibility.

Among the organisations contacted, only Get Together After Serving CIC and Hebron Pentecostal Church attended to assist.

Approximately ten hours after the incident began, police officers attended the scene.

The following morning, disposable cups, bowls and cardboard still marked the place where the elderly man had spent much of the previous day.

This investigation is not an argument that NHS staff should tolerate abuse. They should not. Nor is it an argument that previous violent or abusive behaviour should simply be ignored.

It is, however, a question of safeguarding.

If an elderly man is confused, apparently incapable of caring for himself, unable to stand, repeatedly soiling himself and lying outside the grounds of a hospital, who has responsibility for protecting him?

If previous behaviour has resulted in restrictions, what emergency pathway exists when that same individual later appears to lack capacity or requires urgent medical assessment?

Those are questions Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, North West Ambulance Service, Greater Manchester Police and Rochdale Council's Adult Social Care service should now answer.

Rochdale Daily has contacted all relevant organisations for comment and will publish their responses in full when received.

Until then, one unavoidable question remains.

Is this how the NHS treats its own?

title: Peaceful Pool sessions return to Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre for SEND families
excerpt: Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre is once again offering its popular Peaceful Pool sessions throughout the summer holidays, creating a calm, welcoming and sensory-friendly swimming environment for children and adults with SEND and their families.
content_html:
Families across the Rossendale Valley and Rochdale borough are being invited to enjoy a quieter, more inclusive swimming experience this summer as Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre continues its popular Peaceful Pool sessions.

Designed specifically for children and adults with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), along with their families, the sessions provide a calm, judgement-free environment where everyone can relax, connect and enjoy time together at their own pace.

The initiative recognises that many families can find busy public swimming sessions overwhelming due to noise, bright lighting and sensory stimulation. Peaceful Pool aims to remove those barriers by creating an environment where participants feel comfortable, supported and included.

Sessions will take place every Thursday from 11:30am until 1:00pm throughout the six-week summer holidays.

To create a more accessible experience, the pool environment will feature reduced lighting to provide a calmer atmosphere, while sensory toys and floating aids will be available for swimmers to enjoy. Families are encouraged to use the facilities in whatever way feels right for them, whether that means swimming, playing in the water, paddling at the poolside or simply becoming familiar with the environment.

Organisers say the sessions are all about allowing people to be themselves without fear of judgement.

The promotional campaign explains that many families of children with SEND can often feel judged or cautious about how their child's behaviour may be perceived in public spaces. Peaceful Pool has therefore been designed to offer a welcoming environment where everyone can feel safe, respected and accepted.

The centre's message is simple: 'Everyone is welcome here just as you are.' That philosophy reflects a growing recognition across the leisure sector of the importance of making public facilities more inclusive and accessible for people with additional needs.

Swimming is widely recognised for its physical and mental wellbeing benefits, helping to improve confidence, mobility, coordination and overall fitness while providing an enjoyable activity for the whole family. Creating opportunities for families to access those benefits in a supportive environment can make a significant difference for many people who may otherwise struggle to attend mainstream sessions.

The Peaceful Pool sessions are available at the standard swim admission price, ensuring families can take part without paying a premium for accessible provision.

Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre continues to expand its programme of community-focused activities, with Peaceful Pool forming part of its wider commitment to ensuring local leisure facilities are welcoming and inclusive for residents of all ages and abilities.

Peaceful Pool takes place every Thursday between 11:30am and 1:00pm throughout the six-week summer holidays at Whitworth Leisure & Wellbeing Centre.

title: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh appointed education minister: what his new role means for the borough
excerpt: Paul Waugh remains Rochdale's MP while taking on a second role as a junior education minister. We examine his responsibilities, additional salary and what the appointment could mean locally.
content_html:
Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has joined the Government as a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State in the Department for Education while continuing to represent the constituency in the House of Commons.

The appointment was formally confirmed as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's ministerial changes, with Mr Waugh taking up the post on 22 July 2026. Lucy Powell is the Secretary of State for Education and heads the department in which he will serve.

Mr Waugh now holds two connected public roles. He remains Rochdale's elected Member of Parliament, responsible for representing constituents, handling casework, holding surgeries, speaking on local issues and voting in the Commons. Alongside that work, he is now a junior government minister with responsibilities inside the Department for Education.

There is nothing unusual or constitutionally improper about an MP also serving as a minister. Most ministers in the House of Commons continue to represent their constituencies. His appointment does not create a vacancy, require a by-election or transfer his constituency responsibilities to another MP.

However, the ministerial job will substantially increase his workload. Ministers are expected to attend departmental meetings, study submissions from civil servants, help develop policy, answer parliamentary questions, take legislation through Parliament, meet education organisations and defend government decisions publicly.

That means constituents will reasonably expect reassurance that Rochdale casework and local representation will continue at the same level. Much of an MP's casework is managed by constituency and parliamentary staff, but Mr Waugh remains personally accountable to Rochdale voters and will still be expected to maintain a visible presence in the borough.

His precise policy portfolio has not yet been published by the Department for Education. The official government page currently confirms his rank and appointment but does not list a detailed set of responsibilities. It would therefore be premature to claim that he has direct control of a particular area such as schools, special educational needs, colleges or apprenticeships until the department formally allocates those duties.

As a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, he is one of the department's junior ministers. Such ministers commonly oversee a defined group of policies, represent the department during Commons debates, answer written and oral questions, meet professional bodies and work under the direction of the Education Secretary and more senior ministers.

The Department for Education is responsible for education and children's services in England. Its work includes early years provision, schools, teacher recruitment and retention, the curriculum, children's social care, further education, higher education, apprenticeships and skills.

The appointment could give Rochdale a stronger connection to national education decision-making, although a minister is required to make decisions for the country as a whole rather than favouring their own constituency.

Locally, there are several areas where residents and education providers will watch his work closely. These include special educational needs and disabilities, school funding, teacher recruitment, attendance, college provision, apprenticeships and support for children requiring speech, language and communication services.

Mr Waugh has previously highlighted Rochdale's work on SEND and early speech and language support. In June, after hosting a ministerial visit to the borough, he said his job was to ensure Rochdale received every penny and every bit of support it had earned. His new position places him inside the department responsible for much of that national policy, although ministerial rules may limit how directly he can intervene in individual local funding decisions.

His salary is also expected to increase if he claims the ministerial salary attached to the post. All MPs currently receive a basic annual salary of £98,599. The claimed additional salary for a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State serving in the Commons is £22,375.

That would produce total gross annual pay of £120,974 before tax, National Insurance and pension deductions. Ministerial salaries are separate from parliamentary expenses, which are intended to cover legitimate costs such as employing staff, running offices and travelling for parliamentary duties rather than providing additional personal income.

The increase is paid because ministerial office carries responsibilities beyond those of an ordinary backbench MP. Ministers are members of the Government and are bound by collective responsibility, meaning they are generally expected to support agreed government policy publicly or resign from office.

That obligation can occasionally create tension between the two roles. As Rochdale's MP, Mr Waugh is expected to raise local concerns and challenge decisions affecting his constituents. As a minister, he must also support the Government's education programme and comply with the Ministerial Code.

Having a minister as the local MP can provide greater access to senior figures and a deeper understanding of how government decisions are made. It does not, however, guarantee preferential funding or special treatment for the constituency. Decisions involving grants, schools and public bodies should continue to follow proper departmental processes.

Mr Waugh said he was "delighted" to be joining the Department for Education. His own website announced the appointment on 23 July, a day after the official government record says he took up the role.

The official announcement confirms that he joined an education team led by Lucy Powell, who became Education Secretary on 20 July. Other ministers in the department include Georgia Gould, Baroness Smith of Malvern and Josh MacAlister.

For Rochdale, the main test will be whether Mr Waugh can manage the demands of government while continuing to respond effectively to residents. Constituents should still contact his office about immigration cases, benefits, housing, public services and other matters requiring assistance from their MP.

His appointment raises Rochdale's profile within Westminster and places its MP closer to decisions affecting schools, children and skills across England. The title alone will not determine whether the borough benefits. That will depend on the responsibilities he is eventually given, the policies he helps deliver and whether residents continue to receive effective representation from their MP.

title: Editorial: Justice remains unfinished in Rochdale
excerpt: More than a decade after the Rochdale grooming gang scandal shocked Britain, the perpetrators have been jailed, reforms have been introduced and institutions have apologised. Yet for many survivors and residents, questions about accountability, trust and whether justice has truly been delivered remain unanswered.
content_html:
More than a decade has passed since the Rochdale child sexual exploitation scandal exposed one of the gravest safeguarding failures in modern British history. The men responsible have been convicted and imprisoned, but the question that continues to confront Rochdale is whether justice ended with those convictions.

Successive independent inquiries have reached strikingly similar conclusions. Reviews by Parliament, local safeguarding bodies and independent investigators found that vulnerable children were repeatedly failed by institutions responsible for protecting them. Victims were too often viewed as making 'lifestyle choices' rather than recognised as children subjected to coercion, rape, trafficking and organised sexual exploitation. Information was not consistently shared between agencies, warning signs were missed, organised offending was underestimated and opportunities to intervene were repeatedly lost.

The testimony of survivors remains among the most compelling evidence of those failures. Girls described repeatedly reporting abuse only to be disbelieved, dismissed as troublesome teenagers or treated as willing participants in their own exploitation. Children who regularly went missing were returned to the same environments where offenders continued to target them. Independent reviews concluded that professionals frequently focused on victims' behaviour rather than the methods of coercion used by organised offenders.

The criminal justice system eventually delivered significant convictions. Operation Span resulted in nine men being convicted in 2012 for offences including rape, trafficking and conspiracy to engage in sexual activity with children. Further investigations have led to additional prosecutions linked to historic child sexual exploitation across Greater Manchester. Judges described the offending as calculated, organised and profoundly damaging, recognising that many victims would carry lifelong psychological trauma.

Yet convictions answered only one question: the guilt of the offenders. They did not answer why children were repeatedly failed before those prosecutions ever reached a courtroom.

The official inquiries found that the primary problem was not an absence of legislation. The criminal offences already existed. Rather, agencies failed to recognise organised grooming, safeguarding procedures were inconsistently applied, intelligence was not always effectively shared and vulnerable children were too often judged instead of protected. Some reviews also concluded that concerns about community tensions influenced professional decision-making in certain cases, although they stressed that institutional failures were complex and involved multiple contributing factors.

Political debate over those failures continues today. Sir Keir Starmer has consistently defended his record as Director of Public Prosecutions, pointing to reforms introduced after the Rochdale prosecutions that encouraged prosecutors to focus more closely on suspect behaviour rather than relying heavily on assessments of victim credibility. Nigel Farage has repeatedly argued that institutional accountability remains incomplete and has called for wider national inquiries into organised child sexual exploitation.

Independent MP Rupert Lowe commissioned his own inquiry into grooming gangs, arguing that previous investigations had failed to provide full transparency or accountability. Lowe's report calls for mandatory recording of offender ethnicity, stronger criminal justice responses, improved national data collection and further investigation into institutional failings. While his inquiry does not carry statutory authority, it has become part of the continuing national debate surrounding organised child sexual exploitation and institutional responsibility.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan also faced criticism after asking for clarification during a London Assembly meeting about what was meant by the phrase 'grooming gangs' before responding more broadly on child sexual exploitation. The exchange became part of the wider political discussion over how public authorities describe organised abuse and communicate with victims and the public.

There have unquestionably been improvements since the original scandal. Greater Manchester Police has established dedicated child sexual exploitation capabilities, multi-agency safeguarding arrangements have been strengthened, inspection reports have recognised improvements in identifying vulnerable children and historic offenders continue to face prosecution years after their crimes. Those reforms are significant and should not be dismissed.

However, reform is not the same as accountability.

For many survivors, organisational apologies and revised procedures have never fully addressed the institutional failures identified by successive inquiries. Former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver has repeatedly argued that child sexual exploitation remains a continuing threat and has warned against believing the lessons of Rochdale have been fully learned. She has consistently maintained that safeguarding depends not only on procedures but on professionals who are prepared to challenge assumptions, recognise organised exploitation and place children's welfare above institutional reputation.

Child sexual exploitation has not disappeared. Police forces across England and Wales continue to investigate organised grooming offences while offenders increasingly exploit social media, encrypted messaging platforms, online coercion and county lines criminality. Organised abuse evolves. Safeguarding must evolve with it.

The greatest lesson from Rochdale is not that Britain lacked the legal powers to prosecute offenders. It is that institutions repeatedly failed to use those powers when vulnerable children first asked for help. Children who should have been believed were doubted. Warning signs that should have triggered intervention were overlooked. Opportunities to prevent further abuse were lost.

Rochdale Borough Council has acknowledged profound institutional failings and apologised to survivors. Public bodies have accepted that serious mistakes were made, while successive reforms have sought to strengthen safeguarding and improve inter-agency cooperation. Those changes deserve recognition.

Whether they have fully restored public trust is another question entirely.

Justice cannot be measured solely by the length of prison sentences imposed on offenders. It is also measured by whether institutions learn from catastrophic failure, whether public officials accept responsibility when safeguarding collapses and whether every vulnerable child reporting abuse today can expect to be believed, protected and acted upon without hesitation.

Until survivors believe those standards have been achieved, and until the public is confident that institutional accountability carries meaningful consequences as well as organisational reform, many will continue to conclude that justice in Rochdale remains unfinished.

title: Heat exposes challenges facing Rochdale workers and Britain’s ageing infrastructure
excerpt: Temperatures are forecast to reach around 27°C in Rochdale today, while hotter conditions affect other parts of England. The weather is renewing questions about worker protection, climate change and whether Britain’s buildings and infrastructure are prepared for warmer summers.
content_html:
Warm conditions are presenting renewed challenges for workers in Rochdale and across the country today, raising questions about whether climate change, inadequate infrastructure investment or a combination of both has left Britain poorly prepared for increasingly hot summers.

Temperatures in Rochdale are forecast to rise to approximately 27°C during the afternoon, with the hottest conditions expected between 3pm and 5pm. Although that is below the extreme temperatures recorded during previous heatwaves, it can still create difficult conditions inside poorly ventilated offices, factories, warehouses, workshops and vehicles.

Conditions are hotter in parts of southern and south-eastern England, where temperatures are significantly above those being experienced across Greater Manchester. The contrast means Britain is not facing identical conditions everywhere, but the national trend towards warmer and more frequent hot periods is placing increasing pressure on workplaces and public infrastructure.

Office workers can struggle in buildings with large windows, limited ventilation, sealed windows or insufficient cooling. Computers, lighting and large numbers of people can raise indoor temperatures beyond those recorded outside, leaving employees dealing with fatigue, headaches, dehydration and reduced concentration.

The risks are greater for people undertaking strenuous or outdoor work. Construction workers, roofers, landscapers, refuse collectors, delivery drivers, road crews, agricultural workers and utility engineers may be required to perform physically demanding tasks in direct sunlight while wearing heavy clothing or protective equipment.

Heat stress can develop when the body is unable to regulate its temperature effectively. Symptoms can include tiredness, dizziness, confusion, headaches, excessive sweating, muscle cramps and nausea. More serious cases can lead to heat exhaustion or heatstroke, requiring urgent medical attention.

There is no fixed maximum legal workplace temperature in Britain. The Health and Safety Executive says this is because workplaces vary considerably, with some industries naturally operating in hotter environments. Employers must nevertheless comply with health and safety law, maintain a reasonable working temperature, provide clean and fresh air and assess risks to employees.

For outdoor and physically demanding roles, sensible precautions can include access to drinking water, additional breaks, shaded rest areas, lighter clothing where safety permits and rescheduling the hardest work away from the hottest part of the day. Employers may also need to monitor staff for signs of heat stress and allow workers time to become accustomed to unusually warm conditions.

Whether Britain’s difficulties can be blamed on government underinvestment or climate change is not an either-or question.

Human-driven climate change is increasing the likelihood and severity of hot weather in Britain. Official figures published by the Office for National Statistics show that the average number of hot days during the decade from 2015 to 2024 was nearly double that recorded between 2005 and 2014. The most recent decade was also warmer than previous reference periods.

However, climate change does not explain why so many British workplaces, schools, hospitals, homes and transport systems struggle when temperatures rise. Much of the country’s built environment was designed for a historically cooler climate, while investment in ventilation, shading, insulation, urban trees and other forms of heat adaptation has not consistently kept pace with the changing risk.

The Climate Change Committee has repeatedly warned that Britain is inadequately prepared for the effects of a warmer climate. Its 2026 assessment said hotter heatwaves could eventually cause the overwhelming majority of existing homes to overheat without sufficient adaptation. Although that warning focused primarily on housing, many of the same construction and ventilation problems affect workplaces.

Successive governments of different political parties have therefore inherited and contributed to the problem. Britain’s exposure has developed over decades through ageing buildings, inconsistent adaptation policies and a planning system that has not always treated overheating as a central design concern.

The economic consequences are also significant. Experimental analysis by the Office for National Statistics estimated that hot days caused an average annual productivity loss of approximately £1.2 billion between 1998 and 2021, even after accounting for adaptation. Workers generally complete tasks more slowly in excessive heat, while employers may face disruption, additional breaks, equipment problems and higher cooling costs.

Urban areas can be particularly vulnerable because roads, roofs, concrete and other hard surfaces absorb heat during the day and release it slowly. Trees, parks, rivers and other green or blue spaces provide natural cooling, but their availability varies considerably between communities.

The challenge facing the Government is therefore twofold. Reducing greenhouse-gas emissions remains necessary to limit the severity of future warming, but adaptation is also required because some further climate change is already unavoidable.

That means improving building standards, retrofitting unsuitable properties, expanding tree cover, protecting green space and ensuring schools, hospitals, care facilities, transport networks and workplaces can remain safe during hot weather. Employers must also recognise that heat planning can no longer be treated as an exceptional response reserved for record-breaking temperatures.

Today’s weather in Rochdale is warm rather than unprecedented. Nevertheless, it provides another indication of a challenge that will become increasingly familiar. Climate change is making hot periods more likely, while inadequate preparation determines how disruptive and dangerous those periods become.

The evidence suggests both factors are responsible. The climate is changing, but Britain’s failure to adapt its workplaces and infrastructure quickly enough is increasing the burden placed on office staff, labourers and those whose jobs cannot simply be moved into an air-conditioned room.
source_name: Met Office, Health and Safety Executive, Office for National Statistics and Climate Change Committee

title: Is ketamine becoming a problem in Rochdale? Health leaders warn of a growing concern
excerpt: Health professionals are warning of the growing harms associated with ketamine as national use rises. But what does the picture look like in Rochdale, and why are experts becoming increasingly concerned?
content_html:
Ketamine was once regarded primarily as a nightclub drug, but health professionals, police and addiction specialists say its use has changed dramatically over the past decade. Increasingly, the drug is being used by younger people in a wider range of settings, prompting growing concern about its impact on physical and mental health.

While there is no publicly available evidence to suggest Rochdale has a ketamine problem significantly worse than other parts of Greater Manchester, local authorities recognise substance misuse as an important public health issue and have included drug-related harm as a key priority in the borough's long-term prevention strategy. Rochdale's Preventing Drug and Alcohol Harm Strategy highlights the need to reduce drug-related harm through prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery services.

Ketamine is a Class B controlled drug in the UK. Originally developed as a medical anaesthetic, it produces feelings of detachment and hallucinations when used recreationally. In recent years, it has become increasingly popular because it is often cheaper than cocaine and MDMA, while users mistakenly believe it to be a 'safer' drug.

National evidence suggests that perception is dangerously wrong. The Home Office's latest wastewater analysis estimates ketamine consumption has increased substantially in England in recent years, making it one of the country's most commonly consumed illegal drugs after cocaine.

Doctors are particularly concerned about the long-term physical effects. Repeated ketamine use can cause irreversible damage to the bladder and urinary tract, a condition sometimes referred to as 'ketamine bladder' or ketamine-induced cystitis. Heavy users may experience severe pain, frequent urination, bleeding and, in the most serious cases, permanent bladder damage requiring reconstructive surgery. Medical specialists have reported a significant increase in young patients requiring treatment for these complications.

Mental health professionals also warn that regular ketamine use can lead to dependency, memory problems, anxiety, depression and episodes of psychosis in some individuals. Because the drug affects perception and coordination, users are also at increased risk of accidents, injuries and dangerous behaviour while intoxicated.

Locally, Rochdale Borough Council's Joint Strategic Needs Assessment identifies substance misuse among young adults as an ongoing public health challenge. Hospital admission rates linked to substance misuse among young people remain broadly similar to the national average, while the council notes that vulnerable groups are at greater risk of developing drug-related problems.

Although official figures are not routinely broken down by individual drug at borough level, professionals working in addiction services across Greater Manchester say ketamine now features far more frequently than it did a decade ago. Nationally, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs concluded earlier this year that misuse is increasing and recommended strengthening education, prevention and treatment services while keeping ketamine as a Class B drug.

Parents are encouraged to be aware of the warning signs. These can include sudden mood changes, poor concentration, unexplained urinary problems, nosebleeds caused by snorting powder, secrecy around friendships, declining school or college attendance and unexplained financial difficulties. None of these signs alone necessarily indicate drug use, but experts advise early conversations and support where concerns exist.

Support is available for anyone struggling with drug use. Rochdale residents can access confidential help through local drug and alcohol treatment services without fear of judgement. Health professionals stress that seeking support early greatly improves the chances of recovery and helps prevent long-term physical damage.

The message from health leaders is clear. While ketamine may still carry an image as a recreational party drug, the evidence increasingly shows it can have devastating consequences for both physical and mental health. Prevention, education and early intervention remain the most effective ways of protecting young people across Rochdale borough from the lasting harm associated with its misuse.

title: GCSE results day 2026: What Rochdale parents need to know – and why one set of grades doesn't define a future
excerpt: From college offers to apprenticeships and changing employer expectations, here's everything Rochdale parents need to know before GCSE results day.
content_html:
Thousands of teenagers across Rochdale borough will soon collect one of the most important envelopes of their young lives as GCSE results day approaches.

For many families, results day brings a mixture of excitement, nerves and uncertainty. Parents naturally want the best for their children, but education experts say GCSEs are increasingly becoming just one of several routes into higher education, apprenticeships and long-term careers rather than the single deciding factor they were once perceived to be.

This year's GCSE results will be released on Thursday 20 August, with schools across Rochdale opening to allow students to collect their grades and speak with teachers about their next steps. Students will receive provisional results before certificates are issued later in the year.

For many teenagers, the next destination has already been decided through conditional offers from sixth forms and colleges. Most colleges will honour offers provided students meet the required grades, while admissions teams are usually available on results day to discuss alternatives if results are different from those expected.

Compared with a decade ago, today's post-16 education landscape is far more flexible. Alongside traditional A Levels, students can now choose from T Levels, vocational qualifications, apprenticeships and technical training, giving young people far more options depending on their interests and career ambitions. Greater Manchester has also continued expanding the Greater Manchester Baccalaureate (MBacc), designed to place technical education on an equal footing with academic study while creating clearer pathways into local industries.

Parents often ask whether GCSEs still matter.

The answer is yes—but perhaps not in the way they once did.

GCSEs remain important because they open doors. Most sixth forms, colleges, universities and apprenticeship providers require passes in English Language and Mathematics, while many A Level courses ask for a minimum grade in the subject students wish to study. Employers also continue to value GCSEs as evidence of literacy, numeracy and commitment, particularly when recruiting school leavers with little previous work experience. Ofqual has described GCSEs as a 'passport to opportunity', providing access to further education, apprenticeships and employment.

However, the employment market has changed dramatically. Increasingly, recruiters say experience, practical skills, communication, teamwork and attitude become far more important than GCSE grades as careers progress.

Recruitment specialists consistently report that while GCSEs may be used as an initial screening tool for younger applicants, employers recruiting experienced candidates are far more interested in work history, achievements, technical skills and professional qualifications. In sectors such as construction, logistics, digital technology, engineering, health and social care, apprenticeships have become an increasingly respected route into well-paid careers.

That does not mean students should dismiss their exams. Strong GCSE results can provide greater choice and flexibility, particularly for competitive sixth forms, universities and professional careers such as medicine, dentistry and law. But equally, disappointing grades do not prevent someone building a successful future.

Parents are also encouraged to remember that results day is only one moment in a much longer journey. Colleges regularly help students who narrowly miss entry requirements by suggesting alternative courses, foundation programmes or vocational pathways that still lead towards the same career goals.

For students who do not achieve the grade 4 pass in English or Mathematics, the law requires them to continue studying those subjects alongside most post-16 courses until they achieve the qualification or turn 18. While this can initially feel disappointing, many students successfully improve their grades during college.

Perhaps the biggest change in recent years has been the growing recognition that success comes in many different forms. University is no longer viewed as the only prestigious route after school. Degree apprenticeships, higher apprenticeships and technical qualifications now offer opportunities to earn a salary while gaining nationally recognised qualifications, often avoiding the student debt associated with traditional university study.

For parents, experts recommend focusing on support rather than pressure. Results day can be emotional regardless of the outcome. Celebrating achievements, discussing options calmly and remembering that there are always alternative pathways can help young people make confident decisions about their future.

Whether a student achieves straight grade 9s or faces unexpected disappointment, GCSE results represent the beginning of the next chapter rather than the end of the story. Across Rochdale borough this summer, thousands of young people will take their next step towards sixth form, college, apprenticeships, employment or technical training—and for many, the opportunities available today are broader than ever before.

title: Lives cut short: Remembering the young people lost on Rochdale's roads
excerpt: A look at the tragic loss of young lives on Rochdale's roads since 2020 and the ongoing efforts to improve road safety across the borough.
content_html:
Every fatal road traffic collision leaves behind grieving families, devastated friends and communities asking whether more could have been done to prevent another life being cut short.

Since 2020, a number of young people have tragically lost their lives on roads across Rochdale borough. While every collision has had its own unique circumstances, each has served as a stark reminder that road safety is not simply about statistics – it is about sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, classmates and friends whose futures were taken away far too soon.

One of the most heartbreaking incidents came in April 2025 when six-year-old Myra Tahseen died after being struck by a vehicle on Ashfield Road. Emergency services fought to save her, but she sadly died from her injuries. The tragedy prompted an outpouring of grief across Rochdale, with floral tributes left at the scene and specialist officers supporting her family while investigations continued.

Although fatalities involving children and young people are thankfully rare, they remain one of the leading causes of death for those aged between five and nineteen across the United Kingdom. Rochdale's own Joint Strategic Needs Assessment highlights that land transport collisions remain among the principal causes of death for young people and reports that the borough's rate of children killed or seriously injured on the roads is around 15 per 100,000 population.

Behind every fatal collision lies a complex combination of circumstances. Excessive speed, distraction, impairment through drink or drugs, failure to wear seatbelts, poor weather, inexperience and momentary lapses in concentration can all contribute to devastating outcomes. Road safety experts consistently stress that many serious collisions are preventable through safer driving behaviour.

Young drivers remain disproportionately represented in serious road collisions nationwide. Inexperience, overconfidence and risk-taking behaviour can all increase the likelihood of being involved in a collision, particularly during the first years after passing a driving test. Equally, young pedestrians and cyclists are among the most vulnerable road users, particularly near schools, residential estates and busy roads.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit continues to investigate every fatal collision thoroughly, examining witness statements, CCTV, vehicle data, road conditions and forensic evidence to establish exactly what happened. These investigations often continue for many months before an inquest is held, allowing families to receive answers and, where appropriate, criminal proceedings to take place.

Road safety is not solely the responsibility of drivers. Pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and passengers all have a role to play in reducing risk. Simple decisions such as slowing down in residential areas, putting mobile phones away, wearing seatbelts correctly, using pedestrian crossings where available and remaining alert around schools can make a significant difference.

Across Rochdale borough, organisations continue to work together to improve road safety through engineering improvements, education campaigns, enforcement against dangerous driving and community awareness initiatives. Every serious collision provides lessons that can help prevent future tragedies.

For the families who have lost loved ones, however, those lessons come at an unimaginable cost. Birthdays go uncelebrated, empty seats remain at family tables and communities continue to remember young lives that ended far too soon.

The hope shared by police, road safety campaigners and residents alike is that by learning from these tragedies, encouraging responsible driving and remaining vigilant on every journey, fewer families will have to experience the heartbreak of losing someone they love on Rochdale's roads.

title: Discover the beauty on your doorstep: The spectacular walks of Shawclough and Healey
excerpt: From Healey Dell to the Pennine moors, Shawclough and Healey offer some of Greater Manchester's finest walking routes. Here's how to enjoy them responsibly while discovering the wildlife and landscapes on your doorstep.
content_html:
With rolling moorland, ancient woodland, dramatic valleys and panoramic Pennine views, Shawclough and Healey offer some of the finest walking routes anywhere in Greater Manchester. Just a few minutes from Rochdale town centre, the area provides easy access to miles of public footpaths, bridleways and countryside that attract walkers, runners, cyclists and nature lovers throughout the year.

Whether you're looking for a gentle afternoon stroll or a challenging hike onto the South Pennine moors, there is a route to suit every ability. Healey Dell Nature Reserve remains one of the area's most popular destinations, with its historic railway viaduct, woodland trails and the River Spodden winding through a picturesque valley rich in wildlife. From there, walkers can continue towards Shawclough, Rooley Moor Road, Brown Wardle Hill, Knowl Hill and the Pennine Bridleway, enjoying some of the most impressive views across Rochdale, Rossendale and beyond. The wider area also links into the Rochdale Way and Rossendale Way, providing opportunities for much longer circular walks.

The landscape changes dramatically with the seasons. During late summer, the surrounding moorland is coloured by flowering heather, while ancient dry stone walls, reservoirs and grazing farmland create the classic Pennine scenery that has inspired walkers for generations.

The area is also a haven for wildlife. At this time of year, walkers are likely to spot kestrels hovering above the fields, buzzards circling on thermals, swallows and house martins feeding before beginning their autumn migration, and flocks of goldfinches gathering on seed heads. In the woodlands around Healey Dell, visitors may hear great spotted woodpeckers, nuthatches, wrens, robins and tawny owls after dusk. Lucky walkers may even catch sight of kingfishers along quieter stretches of the River Spodden. Roe deer are regularly seen at dawn and dusk around Healey Dell, Rooley Moor and neighbouring farmland, while foxes, badgers, rabbits and brown hares also inhabit the surrounding countryside.

As enjoyable as these walks are, visitors are reminded that much of the surrounding countryside remains working farmland. Public Rights of Way allow people to cross private land using designated footpaths and bridleways, but walkers should always remain on the marked route unless they are on land with wider access rights. Respecting the Countryside Code helps ensure these routes remain open for everyone to enjoy.

Simple acts of courtesy make a significant difference. Gates should always be left exactly as they are found. If a gate is closed, close it again after passing through. If it has been left open, leave it open. Farmers often manage livestock carefully, and an incorrectly opened or closed gate can allow animals to stray or separate livestock.

Dog owners also have an important responsibility. Even the friendliest dog can frighten livestock, particularly sheep with lambs or cattle with calves. Dogs should be kept under close control and, wherever livestock are present, they should be kept on a lead. If cattle become inquisitive or begin approaching, it is usually safest to release the dog if necessary, as it can outrun livestock and return once the danger has passed.

Walkers are also encouraged to remain vigilant for injured or distressed animals. If you discover a sheep that has rolled onto its back and cannot get up—a situation known as being 'cast' or 'turned over'—or encounter injured cattle, the best course of action is to contact the farmer if they can be identified, or report the location to the local authority or police if there is an immediate welfare concern. Unless you are experienced and it is safe to do so, avoid attempting to handle large livestock yourself.

The natural beauty of Shawclough and Healey depends on everyone doing their part. Taking litter home, avoiding lighting fires, respecting wildlife and staying on established paths all help protect this special landscape for future generations.

For many residents, one of the greatest pleasures of living in Rochdale is having countryside of this quality virtually on the doorstep. In less than an hour, it is possible to walk from peaceful woodland to open Pennine moorland, passing historic landmarks, abundant wildlife and breathtaking viewpoints along the way.

As summer gradually gives way to autumn, there are few better times to lace up your walking boots, head for the hills and rediscover the remarkable countryside that surrounds Shawclough and Healey.

title: Litter blighting Deeplish remains a concern for residents
excerpt: Residents are calling for continued action to tackle litter in Deeplish, with many saying cleaner streets would improve community pride and the appearance of the neighbourhood.
content_html:
Residents in Deeplish are continuing to raise concerns about litter on streets, pavements and alleyways, with many saying more needs to be done to improve the appearance of one of Rochdale's busiest neighbourhoods.

Discarded food packaging, drinks containers, household waste and fly-tipped rubbish have become a familiar sight in some parts of the area, particularly around shopping parades, rear alleyways and heavily used pedestrian routes. While council cleansing teams regularly clear litter and remove illegally dumped waste, many residents say the problem often returns within days.

Litter is more than just an eyesore. Environmental experts warn that rubbish left on streets can block drains, attract vermin, harm wildlife and negatively affect people's perception of their neighbourhood. Research has also suggested that cleaner streets can help improve community pride and reduce further anti-social behaviour.

Rochdale Borough Council says it has enforcement officers patrolling the borough who can issue £75 fixed penalty notices to anyone caught dropping litter. The authority is also responsible for removing litter from public land, emptying public bins and responding to reports of overflowing bins and fly-tipping. Residents can report litter, overflowing bins and illegally dumped waste through the council's online reporting system.

In recent years, the council has also carried out targeted environmental improvement projects in the wider Milkstone and Deeplish ward. These have included deep-cleaning operations, alleyway clearances, vegetation removal and educational campaigns encouraging residents to dispose of waste responsibly. Environmental officers have also visited homes to provide advice on recycling, bulky waste collections and proper waste disposal.

Those projects have delivered visible improvements in some locations. Previous council feedback found many residents believed streets were noticeably cleaner following targeted clean-up initiatives, although some also suggested additional litter bins and continued maintenance would help sustain those improvements.

Community groups say keeping Deeplish clean is a shared responsibility. While enforcement and regular cleansing remain important, they argue lasting improvements depend on residents, businesses and visitors disposing of rubbish responsibly and reporting fly-tipping when it occurs.

The council also supports volunteer litter-picking groups by providing equipment and arranging the collection of rubbish gathered during organised clean-up events, allowing local people to play an active role in improving their neighbourhood.

Many residents believe Deeplish has a strong community spirit and deserves clean, welcoming streets that reflect the pride people take in the area. They hope continued enforcement against littering, regular cleansing operations and greater public awareness will help ensure that progress made through previous environmental improvement projects is not undone.

Anyone who witnesses littering or discovers fly-tipped waste on public land is encouraged to report it to Rochdale Borough Council, helping officers identify problem areas and take enforcement action where appropriate.
