title: Residents raise concerns over anti-social behaviour around Kingsway
excerpt: Residents and businesses are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour around Kingsway, with police identifying retail crime, ASB and road safety as neighbourhood priorities.
content_html:
Residents and businesses around the Kingsway area of Rochdale are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour, saying a minority of offenders are affecting what is otherwise one of the borough's busiest retail and employment destinations.

Kingsway has undergone significant regeneration over the past two decades, transforming into a major business and retail hub with national retailers, industrial estates, distribution centres and hundreds of jobs. Thousands of people visit the area every day to shop, work and access nearby facilities.

However, some residents and businesses say issues including nuisance behaviour, shoplifting, groups congregating outside retail premises, dangerous driving and road safety concerns have become increasingly noticeable in recent years.

Greater Manchester Police has identified retail crime at Kingsway Retail Park, anti-social behaviour and road safety as neighbourhood policing priorities for the area. Officers say they have carried out targeted operations against shoplifting, increased patrols and undertaken road traffic enforcement to tackle motorists committing offences.

Police have confirmed that numerous arrests have been made for shoplifting at Morrisons in recent months, while dedicated traffic operations have also been carried out along Kingsway to improve road safety. Regular police surgeries are also being held at Kingsway Retail Park to allow residents and businesses to discuss local concerns directly with neighbourhood officers.

For businesses operating on Kingsway, anti-social behaviour can have a wider economic impact. Retailers say persistent shoplifting, disorder and nuisance behaviour place additional pressure on staff while affecting customer confidence. Many businesses have invested heavily in CCTV, security staff and crime prevention measures, working alongside Greater Manchester Police to identify prolific offenders.

Residents have also highlighted concerns over speeding, dangerous driving and the use of modified vehicles on Kingsway, particularly during evenings. Although the vast majority of motorists use the road responsibly, police say road safety remains one of their key neighbourhood priorities alongside tackling retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Community safety experts say anti-social behaviour often requires more than enforcement alone. Alongside visible policing, long-term solutions typically involve youth engagement, support for vulnerable individuals, environmental improvements, partnership working with businesses and swift action against repeat offenders.

There have been encouraging signs elsewhere in Rochdale. Greater Manchester Police recently reported significant reductions in anti-social behaviour and wider crime within Rochdale town centre following the introduction of Operation Tetbury, a partnership initiative combining targeted policing with regeneration and community engagement. Officers say anti-social behaviour in the town centre fell by more than 30 per cent during the first year of the operation.

Many residents hope a similarly proactive approach around Kingsway will continue to improve the area, ensuring it remains an attractive destination for shoppers, businesses and investors.

The overwhelming majority of people visiting Kingsway do so without experiencing any problems, and local businesses continue to invest confidently in the area. Nevertheless, residents say continued police visibility, partnership working and prompt action against those responsible for anti-social behaviour will be essential to protecting one of Rochdale's most important commercial centres.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing anti-social behaviour or criminal activity to report it online, by calling 101, or by dialling 999 if there is an immediate risk to life or a crime is in progress.

title: Taxi driver issues safety warning after frightening incident near Littleborough railway station
excerpt: A taxi driver has shared details of a frightening incident near Littleborough railway station in the hope of encouraging colleagues to remain vigilant while waiting for bookings.
content_html:
A taxi driver has urged colleagues across Rochdale borough to remain vigilant after describing a frightening encounter while waiting for his next booking near Littleborough railway station.

The driver said the incident happened shortly after completing an Uber journey from Rochdale Railway Station to a passenger drop-off in Littleborough. After finishing the fare, he parked on a nearby street opposite Littleborough Railway Station while waiting for his next booking.

According to the driver's account, a man described as a white British male aged between 35 and 45 approached the vehicle accompanied by a dog. The driver says the man opened the car door without permission before placing the dog inside the vehicle, along with a bag containing unknown items.

When challenged, the driver alleges the man became aggressive and attempted to damage the vehicle by striking one of the windows. Fearing for his safety, the driver immediately contacted Greater Manchester Police while remaining inside the vehicle.

The driver says the alleged aggression continued while he was speaking to police, prompting him to drive to a safer, busier location near Sainsbury's Local in Littleborough, where he waited for officers to arrive.

Police subsequently attended the scene, took a statement and dealt with the reported incident. Rochdale Daily has approached Greater Manchester Police to establish whether any arrests were made or investigations remain ongoing.

Following the incident, the driver shared his experience publicly in the hope of preventing something similar from happening to others working in the taxi trade.

He is encouraging drivers to avoid waiting for jobs in isolated streets where possible and instead use well-lit locations with passing pedestrians or nearby businesses. He also advises drivers to keep vehicle doors locked while waiting for bookings and to contact police immediately if they feel threatened.

Personal safety is an important consideration for taxi and private hire drivers, many of whom work alone at all hours of the day and night. Drivers frequently find themselves waiting for bookings in unfamiliar locations or transporting passengers they have never previously met. Industry organisations have long encouraged drivers to remain aware of their surroundings, keep communication devices readily available and report suspicious or aggressive behaviour promptly.

While incidents of this nature remain relatively uncommon, they serve as a reminder of the challenges faced by those working in the transport sector. For many drivers, particularly those working evening and overnight shifts, staying alert and choosing safe waiting locations forms an important part of their daily routine.

Anyone who witnesses criminal damage, threatening behaviour or any incident where someone feels at immediate risk should contact Greater Manchester Police on 999 in an emergency, or report non-emergency incidents by calling 101 or using the force's online reporting service.

title: Residents voice concerns over dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road
excerpt: Residents have raised concerns about dangerous driving and alleged street racing on Milkstone Road, with calls for stronger enforcement to improve road safety.
content_html:
Residents and business owners along Milkstone Road are continuing to raise concerns about dangerous driving, excessive speeding and alleged late-night street racing, with many calling for stronger enforcement before someone is seriously injured.

Milkstone Road is one of Rochdale's busiest routes, carrying thousands of vehicles each day while also serving local shops, schools, places of worship and residential streets. For many residents, the road should be a safe route for families, pedestrians and cyclists. However, some say that during evenings and late at night, it can become the scene of drivers accelerating aggressively, revving engines and travelling at excessive speeds.

While there is no evidence to suggest organised street racing is a regular occurrence, residents have reported vehicles appearing to race one another, performing rapid acceleration and driving in a manner they believe is dangerous. Such behaviour can create significant risks for other motorists, pedestrians and nearby residents, particularly on a road with numerous junctions, crossings and side streets.

The concerns reflect a wider national problem. Police forces across the country have stepped up action against illegal street racing and antisocial driving, warning that the behaviour can have devastating consequences. The Government has also strengthened powers allowing police to seize and destroy vehicles used in antisocial driving offences in appropriate circumstances.

Road safety already forms one of the priorities for Greater Manchester Police's Milkstone and Deeplish neighbourhood team. Officers say they are carrying out high-visibility traffic operations, speed enforcement and action against inconsiderate motorists alongside wider work tackling antisocial behaviour and organised crime in the area.

Residents say the issue extends beyond noise. High-speed driving can intimidate pedestrians, discourage people from walking to local businesses and increase the risk of collisions. Milkstone Road is a busy mixed-use corridor where children, elderly residents and shoppers regularly cross the road throughout the day.

National road safety experts have consistently warned that excessive speed dramatically reduces the time available for drivers to react while increasing both the likelihood and severity of collisions. Even where no crash occurs, repeated antisocial driving can have a lasting impact on neighbourhoods through noise, fear and disruption.

Many local residents are now calling for additional measures, including increased police patrols during evening hours, more targeted traffic enforcement, mobile speed checks and continued action against drivers found to be driving dangerously or inconsiderately.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing dangerous driving to report it where it is safe to do so. Dashcam footage, CCTV and details such as registration numbers, locations and times can all assist officers in identifying offenders. Residents should always call 999 if they believe there is an immediate danger to life or serious risk to road users.

For most drivers, Milkstone Road is simply another journey home or to work. However, residents hope that continued enforcement and responsible driving will ensure the road remains safe for everyone who lives, works and travels through one of Rochdale's busiest neighbourhoods.

title: Kirkholt and the fight against knife crime: why prevention matters as much as policing
excerpt: Knife crime remains a concern for many families in Kirkholt, but police, youth workers and community groups say prevention, education and opportunity are just as important as enforcement in keeping young people safe.
content_html:
Knife crime remains one of the issues that concerns many families across Kirkholt and the wider Rochdale borough. While high-profile incidents often make headlines, community leaders, police and youth organisations all agree that preventing young people from carrying knives in the first place is just as important as enforcing the law against those who do.

Although Rochdale has lower levels of knife crime than several other parts of Greater Manchester, it continues to experience incidents involving bladed weapons, particularly in areas facing higher levels of deprivation. The borough's Strategic Threat Assessment notes that knife crime is more common in town centres and some residential neighbourhoods where poverty is greatest, while young people are disproportionately affected as both victims and offenders. It also found that some children told youth workers they carried knives because they believed it offered protection or improved their image among peers.

For communities such as Kirkholt, the challenge is not simply about policing but understanding why some young people feel the need to carry a weapon. Youth workers and charities frequently point to a combination of social pressures, fear of becoming a victim, exploitation by organised criminals, school exclusion, adverse childhood experiences and limited opportunities as factors that can increase vulnerability.

Greater Manchester Police has continued to target violent crime through proactive neighbourhood policing, stop-and-search powers where legally justified and intelligence-led operations against drug dealing and organised crime. Officers covering Balderstone and Kirkholt currently identify drug dealing, off-road bikes and wider neighbourhood crime as local priorities, with regular patrols aimed at disrupting criminal activity and reassuring residents.

There have also been encouraging signs across the borough. Greater Manchester Police says knife crime in Rochdale reduced during the second half of 2024 compared with the first six months of the year, while more than 100 knives were surrendered through permanent amnesty bins installed at local police stations. Officers say removing weapons from circulation is one part of a broader strategy to reduce serious violence.

Community organisations argue, however, that enforcement alone cannot solve the problem. Providing safe places for young people to spend time, investing in youth services, sports clubs and mentoring programmes, and creating better employment opportunities are all seen as essential to reducing the long-term appeal of gangs and weapon carrying.

Parents also have an important role. Talking openly about peer pressure, recognising changes in behaviour and encouraging children to seek help if they feel threatened can all help prevent situations from escalating. Schools across Greater Manchester continue to work alongside police and youth services to educate pupils about the devastating consequences of carrying knives, not only for victims but for those who choose to carry them.

For most people living in Kirkholt, knife crime is not something they encounter in everyday life. The vast majority of residents simply want safe streets, strong communities and opportunities for young people to succeed. Nevertheless, every incident involving a knife has the potential to leave lasting consequences for families and neighbourhoods.

Reducing knife crime ultimately depends on a combination of effective policing, early intervention and community support. While officers continue to target those involved in serious violence, many local organisations believe the greatest success will come from ensuring fewer young people ever feel the need to pick up a knife in the first place.

title: Why are so many HMOs in Spotland? The debate over shared housing in Rochdale
excerpt: Spotland has one of the highest concentrations of Houses in Multiple Occupation in Rochdale borough. But why has the area become a hotspot for shared housing, and what does it mean for residents?
content_html:
Walk through parts of Spotland and it quickly becomes apparent that the area has a far higher concentration of Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) than many other parts of Rochdale borough. Once occupied by single families, many larger Victorian and Edwardian terraced properties have gradually been converted into shared accommodation, making Spotland one of the borough's most significant clusters of HMOs.

The trend has become an increasingly important issue for residents, landlords and councillors alike. While HMOs provide an important source of affordable accommodation for many people, questions continue to be raised about whether too many are concentrated in particular neighbourhoods and what effect that has on local communities.

A House in Multiple Occupation is a property occupied by people from more than one household who share facilities such as kitchens or bathrooms. Larger HMOs with five or more occupants have long required mandatory licences, while since April 2025 Rochdale Council has expanded its additional licensing scheme to include many smaller HMOs with three or four occupants across the borough. The authority says the scheme is intended to improve housing standards, fire safety and property management.

Spotland's high concentration has developed over many years rather than overnight. Much of the housing stock consists of relatively large terraced homes close to Rochdale town centre, public transport, local shops and employment opportunities. Those characteristics make the area attractive for shared housing, particularly for single working adults, people on lower incomes and those needing flexible rented accommodation.

Supporters of HMOs argue they perform an essential role in the local housing market. They provide accommodation for key workers, young people leaving home, people whose relationships have broken down, those moving into the area for work and residents who simply cannot afford to rent an entire property on their own. With housing affordability remaining a challenge across Greater Manchester, shared accommodation is often one of the few realistic options available.

Critics, however, argue that excessive concentrations of HMOs can fundamentally change the character of established residential streets. Residents have raised concerns over increased parking pressures, higher population turnover, refuse management, antisocial behaviour linked to a minority of poorly managed properties and the gradual reduction in the number of traditional family homes available to buy.

Not every HMO creates problems. Many are professionally managed, well maintained and occupied by tenants who contribute positively to the local community. Councils and housing organisations frequently stress that poor management, rather than the concept of shared housing itself, is often at the heart of complaints.

Recognising those concerns, Rochdale Borough Council operates a licensing regime designed to ensure HMOs meet minimum standards covering fire precautions, room sizes, kitchen and bathroom facilities, property management and tenant safety. Licensed HMOs are recorded on a public register, allowing residents to check whether qualifying properties have been licensed.

The wider debate is about balance. Most housing experts accept that HMOs form an important part of the housing mix, but many also argue that large numbers concentrated within relatively small areas can place additional pressure on local services and alter neighbourhood dynamics. Achieving the right balance between providing affordable accommodation and maintaining stable, mixed communities remains one of the key challenges facing local authorities.

Spotland sits at the centre of that discussion in Rochdale. For some, its concentration of shared housing demonstrates the borough's ability to provide affordable homes for a diverse population. For others, it illustrates why councils should have stronger planning powers to prevent excessive clustering and preserve the long-term character of residential streets.

As demand for affordable rented accommodation continues to grow, the debate surrounding HMOs is unlikely to disappear. Future planning decisions, licensing enforcement and investment in housing quality will all play a part in determining whether areas such as Spotland can successfully balance the needs of tenants, landlords and long-established residents alike.

title: Heywood MP congratulates Bev Craig and calls for stronger investment in the north of the borough
excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Mayor of Greater Manchester, with both Labour politicians expected to work together on transport, regeneration and investment priorities across the borough.
content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on her election as Mayor of Greater Manchester, pledging to work closely with the new mayor to secure investment, improve transport and strengthen opportunities for communities across the constituency.

In a public letter following the mayoral election, Blundell said voters had 'reaffirmed their belief that only Labour can deliver on hopes for a fairer Greater Manchester that works for everyone'. She added that she looked forward to working with the new mayor to grow the economic and cultural future of towns including Bamford, Castleton, Heywood, Middleton, Norden and Spotland.

The MP said her priorities remain focused on creating 'a positive future' for both towns and their residents, supporting jobs, culture and regeneration while responding to the wishes of local communities.

Transport featured heavily in her message. Blundell described the current journey from Heywood into central Manchester by public transport as 'unacceptable', saying many young professionals and families need a quicker and more reliable connection to the city. She reiterated her support for extending Metrolink to Heywood, noting that previous commitments had suggested 'spades in the ground' by 2028, and called for continued confidence in delivering the project.

She also welcomed the success of the Bee Network but stressed that towns outside Manchester city centre must not be left behind. Buses and future tram connections, she argued, both have an important role to play in improving connectivity across the constituency.

Blundell highlighted the opportunities presented by the Mayoral Development Corporations planned for Middleton and Atom Valley, describing them as exciting regeneration projects that could combine investment with skills development for both young and older residents. She said it was essential that local people were first in line to benefit from the jobs and opportunities created by future investment.

For residents across Heywood and the wider Rochdale borough, the relationship between the new Mayor and the local Labour MP could prove significant. With both politicians representing the same party, supporters argue there may be greater scope for joined-up working between Westminster, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and local councils when bidding for funding, infrastructure projects and devolved investment.

Whether that political alignment ultimately translates into tangible improvements remains to be seen, but transport projects, regeneration schemes and skills investment are all areas where cooperation between regional and national politicians can help unlock funding and accelerate decision-making.

The timing is particularly important for Rochdale Borough Council. The authority has previously warned of significant long-term financial pressures, with forecasts indicating a funding gap that could reach around £16 million by the end of the decade if additional savings or funding are not identified. While the Mayor of Greater Manchester does not directly control council finances, the Combined Authority plays an increasingly important role in distributing regeneration funding, transport investment, housing programmes, brownfield development grants and skills funding across the city-region.

That means a strong working relationship between the Mayor, local MPs and council leaders could improve the borough's chances of securing external investment for projects that might otherwise place further pressure on local budgets. Investment in transport infrastructure, town-centre regeneration and employment initiatives can help stimulate economic growth, attract private investment and broaden the local tax base over time.

However, the partnership alone cannot solve every financial challenge. Local government funding remains largely determined by central government, while council tax income, business rates and rising demand for statutory services continue to place significant pressure on council budgets across England.

Ultimately, constituents will judge the success of the new political partnership not by the warm words exchanged after the election, but by whether it delivers visible improvements. Faster public transport, investment in Heywood and Middleton, better roads, stronger town centres, more employment opportunities and increased funding for local services are among the outcomes residents will hope to see over the coming years.

With both Elsie Blundell and Bev Craig committed to Labour's vision for Greater Manchester, attention now turns from congratulations to delivery. The coming mayoral term will determine whether that political alignment results in lasting benefits for communities across Heywood, Middleton and the wider Rochdale borough.

title: Milnrow author helping children cope with grief through heartfelt storybooks
excerpt: Milnrow author Jane Somers is helping children understand bereavement and pet loss through two beautifully illustrated storybooks, while donating hundreds of copies to hospitals and hospices.
content_html:
A Milnrow author is helping children navigate some of life's most difficult moments through a pair of beautifully illustrated books exploring bereavement and the loss of much-loved pets.

Jane Somers has written two children's books, *Look For The Robin* and *Over Rainbow Bridge*, with the aim of providing comfort, reassurance and hope for young readers experiencing grief.

Drawing on gentle storytelling and colourful illustrations, Jane's books tackle subjects that many families find difficult to discuss, helping children understand loss in an age-appropriate and compassionate way.

Her first book, *Look For The Robin*, tells the story of a friendly robin who reminds grieving children that the special people they have lost are still watching over them and that they continue to be loved. The book has resonated with families, schools and support organisations, with Jane using proceeds from sales to give something back to the community.

Thanks to the support of readers, she has now donated more than 200 copies of the book to hospitals, hospices and other worthy causes, helping children facing bereavement access the story free of charge. Customers ordering directly from her website also receive a handmade robin clay heart trinket as a keepsake.

Jane's second book, *Over Rainbow Bridge*, focuses on another form of grief that is often underestimated – the loss of a family pet. Written in rhyme and accompanied by warm illustrations, the story follows the bond between children and their beloved animals, reassuring young readers that although their pet has crossed Rainbow Bridge, the love and memories they shared remain forever.

The book aims to help parents start conversations about pet loss in a gentle, positive way, recognising that the death of a much-loved animal is often a child's first experience of bereavement. Every copy purchased through Jane's online store includes a complimentary bookmark.

Child psychologists have long recognised the importance of helping children understand grief through honest but reassuring conversations. Books can provide a safe and accessible way for young readers to explore difficult emotions, ask questions and recognise that feelings such as sadness, confusion and loss are a normal part of bereavement.

Jane says her ambition has always been to create stories that offer comfort while giving families practical tools to support children during challenging times. By combining uplifting messages with beautiful illustrations, she hopes her books provide reassurance that love continues even after someone, or a cherished pet, has gone.

Both books retail at £9.99, excluding postage and packaging, and are available directly through Jane's website. As well as supporting an independent local author, every purchase helps her continue donating copies to hospitals, hospices and organisations supporting bereaved children.

Jane's work is another example of the creativity found within Rochdale borough, using the power of storytelling not only to entertain but to make a genuine difference in the lives of local families and children across the country.

title: Brass band tradition returns to Hare Hill Park this September
excerpt: Friends of Hare Hill Park are inviting residents to enjoy a free afternoon of brass band music on 6 September, celebrating one of the borough's most treasured historic parks and its long musical tradition.
content_html:
The sound of brass music will once again fill Hare Hill Park this autumn as the Friends of Hare Hill Park invite residents to enjoy an afternoon of live music in one of Rochdale borough's most historic green spaces.

The free concert will take place on Saturday, 6 September, from 3pm until 5pm at the park's historic bandstand, continuing a tradition of open-air performances that has entertained generations of local families. Visitors are encouraged to bring a picnic blanket or folding chair and enjoy an afternoon of music surrounded by the park's award-winning gardens.

The event has been organised by the Friends of Hare Hill Park, a volunteer-led community group established more than 14 years ago to help preserve, improve and promote the Edwardian park. During that time, the group has played a major role in securing funding, restoring historic features and ensuring the park remains one of the borough's best-loved public spaces. Their work has helped attract more than £250,000 towards restoration projects, including improvements to many of the park's original Victorian and Edwardian features. Today, Hare Hill Park proudly holds Green Flag status, recognising it as one of the country's best-managed parks.

Although often associated with Milnrow because of its close proximity, Hare Hill Park actually sits in the heart of neighbouring Littleborough. The park was created during the Victorian era alongside Hare Hill House before the estate was sold to Littleborough Urban District Council in 1900, allowing it to become the public park enjoyed by residents today.

Among its most recognisable landmarks is the Grade II-listed bandstand, presented to the people of Littleborough by local benefactor James Cryer in 1902 to commemorate the coronation of King Edward VII. More than 120 years later, it remains the centrepiece for community concerts and one of the park's most photographed historic features.

Over the decades, Hare Hill Park has welcomed countless visitors, community celebrations and civic events. The grounds have long been a venue for brass band concerts, fêtes, remembrance events, sporting activities and family gatherings, making it one of the social hearts of Littleborough and the surrounding Pennine communities.

Brass banding itself forms an important part of the area's industrial heritage. Mill towns across Lancashire and Greater Manchester developed proud brass band traditions during the nineteenth century, with local bands providing entertainment at parks, public celebrations and civic occasions. That heritage remains alive today, with Milnrow Band—founded in 1869—continuing to enjoy national success, recently earning promotion back to the prestigious British Open Championship following victory at the 2026 Grand Shield competition.

Friends of Hare Hill Park say they hope residents from across Rochdale borough will come along to enjoy an afternoon of live music while supporting the park and the volunteers who work throughout the year to keep it looking its best.

With its beautifully restored bandstand, formal gardens, mature trees and rich history, Hare Hill Park provides an ideal backdrop for a traditional brass band concert. For many visitors, it offers the chance to enjoy not only live music but one of the borough's finest historic parks, whose heritage continues to be protected by a dedicated group of local volunteers.

The concert is free to attend and takes place on Saturday, 6 September, between 3pm and 5pm.

title: One man became one walk – now Rochdale's Men Walking and Talking group hopes others will join him
excerpt: A new Men Walking and Talking group has launched in Rochdale, offering men a safe, informal place to meet, walk and talk as organisers hope to tackle loneliness, improve mental wellbeing and reduce the stigma surrounding men's mental health.
content_html:
A simple walk can sometimes be the first step towards changing a life.

That's the message behind Men Walking and Talking, the national Community Interest Company helping men support one another through conversation, companionship and fresh air. The organisation recently launched its Rochdale group, offering a free weekly walk where men can meet without pressure, judgement or the expectation that they have to talk if they don't want to. The walks take place every Thursday evening from Rochdale Cenotaph and are open to all men, with no booking required.

The Rochdale group's organiser recently reflected on one of the challenges facing any new community initiative – sometimes the first person to turn up is the organiser themselves. In recent weeks he has often found himself walking alone, but says he'll continue turning up each Thursday because he believes someone who needs the group will eventually come.

That quiet determination reflects the purpose of Men Walking and Talking. The organisation was founded on the belief that men often find it easier to open up while walking side by side than sitting face-to-face. There is no expectation to share personal struggles, but there is always the opportunity to chat if someone feels ready.

Research has consistently shown that regular physical activity can play an important role in supporting mental wellbeing. Walking outdoors has been linked to reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression, lower stress levels and improved mood. Spending time in nature, exercising regularly and building social connections can all contribute positively to mental health, while loneliness and social isolation are recognised risk factors for poor mental wellbeing.

For many men, however, talking about mental health remains difficult. Although attitudes have improved in recent years, stigma still prevents some people from seeking support. Organisations such as Men Walking and Talking aim to break down those barriers by creating informal spaces where conversation develops naturally rather than feeling like therapy.

The need for initiatives like this remains significant. Suicide continues to be one of the leading causes of death among men under the age of 50 in the UK, with men accounting for around three-quarters of all registered suicides nationally. Behind every statistic are families, friends and communities left dealing with unimaginable loss.

Groups such as Men Walking and Talking cannot replace professional mental health services, but they can provide something equally valuable – connection. A friendly face, a shared walk and the knowledge that someone else understands can make a real difference for people who may otherwise feel isolated.

Community is another important part of the group's mission. Beyond improving physical fitness, regular walks help people build friendships, strengthen local networks and create a sense of belonging. Many participants across the country say they first attended for the walk but kept returning because of the people they met along the way.

The Rochdale organiser hopes more local men will consider giving the group a try. There is no membership, no pressure to speak and no expectation to explain why you've come. Whether someone wants to chat openly, listen quietly or simply enjoy an evening walk with others, they are welcome.

If you are struggling with your mental health, you do not have to face it alone. If you are having thoughts of suicide or feel unable to keep yourself safe, call 999 immediately or go to your nearest Accident and Emergency department. You can also contact Samaritans free of charge on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, or reach out to CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably) on 0800 58 58 58 or through its webchat service. If your situation is not an emergency but you need support, speak to your GP or contact NHS 111 for advice.

Sometimes the hardest part is taking the first step. For one Rochdale volunteer, that first step has meant walking alone while waiting for others to join him. He hopes that, before long, those solitary walks will become conversations shared with men who simply needed someone to walk beside.

title: Norden's hidden gem: Manchester fine dining right here in Rochdale
excerpt: Forget the drive into Manchester. Stocco in Norden is proving that one of Greater Manchester's finest dining experiences can be found right here in Rochdale.
content_html:
When people think of fine dining, they often picture Manchester city centre, Spinningfields or the Northern Quarter. But tucked away in the village of Norden is a restaurant quietly proving that you don't have to travel into the city for an exceptional dining experience.

Stocco, on Edenfield Road, has rapidly established itself as one of Rochdale's standout restaurants, combining contemporary Italian cuisine with stylish surroundings and attentive service that would not look out of place in one of Manchester's best-known dining districts.

Occupying the former Mezbaan site, the restaurant has transformed the building into a modern Italian-inspired venue featuring elegant interiors, a spacious cocktail bar, outdoor terrace seating and room for more than 100 diners. Free parking is available nearby, making it an attractive alternative to the expense and inconvenience of travelling into Manchester for a special meal.

The menu blends traditional Italian cooking with modern British influences, offering everything from freshly prepared pasta and seafood dishes to premium steaks, artisan antipasti and seasonal chef's specials. Ingredients are sourced from local suppliers wherever possible, while speciality products are imported directly from Italy to retain authentic flavours.

Whether you're looking for a relaxed lunch, an evening celebration, cocktails with friends or a romantic meal, Stocco offers a level of quality and atmosphere that many diners would normally expect to find much closer to Manchester city centre.

Its arrival has also helped strengthen Norden's growing reputation as one of Rochdale borough's premier destinations for independent food and drink. Over recent years, the village has developed a thriving hospitality scene, attracting visitors from across Greater Manchester, Rossendale and Lancashire who are increasingly discovering what local residents have known for years.

Since opening, Stocco has built a loyal following, with many customers praising both the quality of the food and the welcoming service. The restaurant has become a popular choice for birthdays, anniversaries, family gatherings and business lunches, while its stylish décor and contemporary feel have made it equally appealing for casual dining.

Perhaps one of Stocco's biggest advantages is convenience. Instead of battling Manchester traffic, paying city-centre parking charges or relying on trains and trams, diners can enjoy a high-end restaurant experience just minutes from Rochdale town centre.

For residents of Rochdale, Bury, Rossendale and the surrounding areas, it is another reminder that outstanding dining experiences don't always require a trip into the city. Sometimes, one of the region's best-kept culinary secrets is much closer to home.

So, the next time you're considering booking a table in Manchester, it might be worth looking north instead. Tucked away in the heart of Norden is a restaurant that delivers city-quality dining with village charm—making it one of Rochdale's true hidden gems.

title: Warning issued after damaged footbridge discovered near Paper House in Norden
excerpt: A snapped wooden plank has left part of the footbridge near the Paper House in Norden damaged, with walkers being urged to take extra care and consider alternative routes until repairs are carried out.
content_html:
Walkers are being urged to take extra care after part of the footbridge near the Paper House in Norden was found to have been damaged.

A wooden plank on the bridge has snapped in half, creating a potential trip hazard for anyone crossing, particularly during busy periods or in poor light. Residents using the route are being advised to slow down, watch their footing and take extra care until repairs can be carried out.

The bridge forms part of a popular walking route used by local residents, dog walkers and visitors exploring the countryside around Norden. With the area attracting large numbers of people during the summer months, the damage could present a risk if left unattended.

Anyone with young children, pushchairs or limited mobility may wish to consider using an alternative route where possible until the bridge has been repaired. Nearby public footpaths and road crossings provide alternative access around the area, although some routes may take slightly longer.

Residents are encouraged to report the damage to the relevant authority if it has not already been logged, helping ensure repairs can be scheduled as quickly as possible.

Until then, anyone planning to use the bridge is asked to remain vigilant, take care when crossing and look out for other walkers who may not have seen the damaged section.

title: Mayor praises Merhaba Festival as 'a wonderful celebration of community'
excerpt: The Mayor of Rochdale has thanked organisers, volunteers and visitors following the Merhaba Festival, describing the event as 'a wonderful celebration of culture, community and togetherness'.
content_html:
"What a fantastic day at the Merhaba Festival. As Mayor of Rochdale, and alongside the Mayoress, I was absolutely delighted to attend and see Rochdale Town Hall Square come alive with such a vibrant celebration of culture, community and togetherness.

There truly was something for everyone. From the delicious food and unique artisan stalls to the live entertainment and welcoming atmosphere, it was wonderful to see people of all ages and backgrounds coming together to enjoy such a special event. The smiles, the laughter and the incredible sense of community made for a truly memorable day.

Events like the Merhaba Festival showcase everything that is great about our borough. They provide an opportunity to learn about different cultures, support local businesses and community organisations, and strengthen the friendships that make Rochdale such a welcoming place to live.

I would like to offer my heartfelt thanks to all of the sponsors, partners and volunteers whose hard work and dedication made this festival possible. Events of this scale simply do not happen without the commitment of so many people working tirelessly behind the scenes. Your efforts have created an event that the whole borough can be proud of.

I also want to thank everyone who attended. Your enthusiasm, kindness and willingness to come together created a warm, welcoming and inclusive atmosphere throughout the day. It was inspiring to see families, friends and visitors enjoying everything the festival had to offer while celebrating the rich diversity that makes Rochdale so special.

As Mayor, I firmly believe Rochdale is at its very best when we celebrate our different cultures, support one another and come together as one community. The Merhaba Festival was a wonderful example of exactly that spirit.

There was great food, fantastic stalls, excellent entertainment and, above all, an amazing atmosphere that could be felt throughout the Town Hall Square from start to finish.

Thank you once again to everyone who helped make the Merhaba Festival such an outstanding success. I am already looking forward to seeing it return next year and to celebrating with our communities once again."

title: Littleborough RUFC invites more girls to discover rugby as women's game continues to boom
excerpt: Littleborough RUFC is inviting girls from Year 6 to under-18 level to try rugby this summer, as the sport continues to grow in popularity thanks to the success of England's Red Roses and increasing awareness of the physical and mental health benefits of team sport.
content_html:
Littleborough Rugby Union Football Club is encouraging girls from across Rochdale borough to give rugby a try this summer, as participation in the women's and girls' game continues to grow at every level of the sport.

The club is holding open training sessions every Tuesday from 6pm until 7pm at its Rakewood Road ground in Littleborough, welcoming girls from Year 6 through to under-18 level. Organisers say there is no commitment required, with players of all abilities invited to come along, meet new friends and experience rugby in a supportive and inclusive environment.

The sessions are designed to introduce newcomers to the sport while allowing experienced players to develop their skills in a fun, welcoming atmosphere. Coaches are keen to stress that previous rugby experience is not necessary, with the emphasis firmly on enjoyment, teamwork and building confidence.

Over the past decade, girls' rugby has experienced remarkable growth across England. The Rugby Football Union has invested heavily in the women's and girls' game, with thousands more young people now playing regularly at schools and grassroots clubs. Many local clubs have expanded their junior girls' sections in response to increasing demand, creating more opportunities than ever before for young female players.

The sport has also benefited from the growing profile of the Red Roses, England's national women's rugby team. Consistently ranked among the best teams in the world, the Red Roses have inspired a new generation of players through their success on the international stage. Record-breaking attendances at Women's Six Nations matches and Rugby World Cup fixtures have demonstrated just how rapidly interest in women's rugby has grown, with elite players increasingly becoming role models for young girls considering taking up the sport.

That success at the highest level has filtered down into communities across the country. Grassroots clubs such as Littleborough RUFC have seen increasing interest from girls looking to get involved, whether for competition, fitness or simply to make new friends.

Beyond the physical benefits of exercise, rugby is widely recognised for the positive impact it can have on mental wellbeing. Taking part in team sports has been linked to reduced feelings of isolation, improved self-esteem and greater confidence, while the friendships formed through regular training and matches often provide valuable support networks for young people.

Coaches also point to the life skills rugby helps develop. Communication, resilience, leadership, discipline and respect for teammates and opponents are central values within the game, with many parents saying participation helps children grow in confidence both on and off the pitch.

The social aspect of rugby is another major attraction. Unlike many sports where players can feel under pressure from the outset, grassroots rugby clubs often place a strong emphasis on creating welcoming environments where everyone can progress at their own pace. That approach is reflected in Littleborough's message that all abilities are welcome and that there is no obligation to commit after attending a session.

The club hopes more girls from across Rochdale, Littleborough, Milnrow, Wardle and the surrounding communities will take the opportunity to experience the sport over the summer. Open training sessions allow newcomers to meet coaches and players, learn the basics and decide whether rugby is the right fit for them before the new season begins.

Training takes place every Tuesday between 6pm and 7pm at Littleborough RUFC, OL15 0AP. Girls in Year 6 through to under-18 level are invited to attend, with organisers encouraging anyone interested to simply come along and give it a go. For further information, prospective players or parents can contact Andy on 07990 744348.

As women's rugby continues to enjoy unprecedented growth across England, clubs such as Littleborough RUFC are hoping to inspire the next generation of players while demonstrating that the game offers far more than competition alone. For many young people, it can provide lasting friendships, improved wellbeing, greater confidence and the chance to become part of a thriving local sporting community.

title: Record month for The Strand Community Café as community support continues to grow
excerpt: The Strand Community Café has celebrated its busiest month ever, introducing new outdoor seating, a book swap, a £1.50 children's menu and a family duck-hunting competition while thanking the community for its continued support.
content_html:
The Strand Community Café in Kirkholt is celebrating its busiest month since opening, with volunteers thanking customers, supporters and local organisations for helping the community venue continue to grow.

The café says the past month has been its most successful to date, with increasing numbers of local residents visiting for breakfast, lunch, daily specials and community activities. Managers say the continued support from customers has allowed them to introduce new initiatives while expanding what the café can offer local people.

One of the highlights of the month was the café's World Cup Competition, organised in partnership with its sister venue, The Hive at the Million Pavilion. Together, the two cafés distributed 60 back-to-school packs to local children, helping families prepare for the new school year.

The café has also invested in additional outdoor seating, providing more space for visitors to enjoy refreshments during the warmer months. A newly introduced Book Swap Club has quickly become a popular feature, encouraging visitors to bring along books they have finished and exchange them for something new to read.

Food continues to be at the heart of the café's success. Daily specials have proved particularly popular with regular customers, while the café says its freshly prepared bacon sandwiches remain one of its biggest sellers, with demand showing no signs of slowing.

With the summer holidays now underway, The Strand Community Café has also introduced a £1.50 children's menu in a bid to provide affordable meals for local families during the school break. The initiative forms part of the café's wider commitment to ensuring the venue remains accessible to everyone in the community.

Perhaps the most unusual attraction currently drawing visitors through the doors is the café's new 'How Many Ducks?' competition. Dozens of small rubber ducks have been hidden in plain sight throughout the café, challenging customers of all ages to see how many they can spot during their visit.

The light-hearted competition has quickly become a talking point among visitors, particularly younger customers, adding another family-friendly activity alongside the café's food and community events.

In a message thanking supporters, the team said the café's success would not have been possible without the continued backing of its loyal customers, volunteers and partners. Special thanks were given to Rochdale Boroughwide Housing for placing its trust in HMR Circle – The Volunteer Drivers Service to manage the café, alongside the community hall and kitchen facilities at The Strand in Kirkholt.

The café has become more than simply a place to eat, evolving into an important community hub where residents can meet friends, enjoy affordable meals and take part in local activities. Initiatives such as the Book Swap Club, children's competitions and low-cost family meals reflect its growing role in supporting the wider Kirkholt community.

With record visitor numbers, expanding facilities and a busy programme of community initiatives, The Strand Community Café says it is looking forward to building on its success throughout the rest of the year. In the meantime, anyone visiting is being encouraged to enjoy a bite to eat, browse the books and see just how many hidden rubber ducks they can find.

title: Hundreds enjoy sunshine, music and family fun at Springhill Hospice Summer Garden Celebration
excerpt: Families, supporters and volunteers gathered at Springhill Hospice for its annual Summer Garden Celebration, enjoying live music, games, food and award-winning gardens while raising vital funds for hospice care.
content_html:
Springhill Hospice welcomed families, supporters and members of the local community to its annual Summer Garden Celebration on Sunday, with visitors enjoying an afternoon of live entertainment, garden games, artisan stalls and fundraising in the Hospice's award-winning grounds.

Running from 11am until 3pm, the free family-friendly event once again opened the Hospice's gardens to the public, giving visitors the opportunity to explore the landscaped grounds while supporting one of Rochdale's best-loved charities. Adult visitors were invited to make a suggested £2 donation, with proceeds helping to fund the specialist palliative and end-of-life care provided by Springhill Hospice.

Throughout the day, the Hospice grounds were filled with families enjoying live music, children's entertainment, traditional garden games and a wide variety of food, drink and shopping stalls. Local traders offered seasonal produce, decorative gifts and artisan products, while visitors relaxed in the sunshine and explored the colourful gardens maintained by the Hospice's gardening team.

The Summer Garden Celebration has become one of Springhill Hospice's most popular community fundraising events, combining a relaxed family day out with an opportunity for residents to learn more about the Hospice's work and the services it provides to patients and families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton and the surrounding areas.

Many visitors took the opportunity to browse the Hospice's gardens, which have received national recognition in recent years for their design and maintenance. The gardens provide an important therapeutic environment for patients and families throughout the year, offering peaceful outdoor spaces where people can spend time together during difficult periods in their lives.

Volunteers, staff and supporters were on hand throughout the afternoon to welcome guests, assist with activities and help raise vital funds. Events such as the Summer Garden Celebration play an important role in supporting the Hospice, which relies heavily on charitable donations and community fundraising to continue providing its specialist care free of charge.

The event attracted families of all ages, with children enjoying games and entertainment while adults explored the various stalls and food outlets. Live music throughout the afternoon helped create a relaxed festival atmosphere as visitors gathered across the Hospice grounds.

Ahead of the event, organisers had promised 'a spectacular day' featuring garden games, live music and delicious food, and Sunday's celebration appeared to deliver exactly that as supporters turned out to enjoy the Hospice's annual summer gathering.

Springhill Hospice provides specialist palliative and end-of-life care for people living with life-limiting illnesses across Rochdale and the surrounding boroughs. As an independent charity, it receives only part of its funding from the NHS, with the majority raised through donations, fundraising events, retail income and the ongoing support of the local community.

The success of events such as the Summer Garden Celebration reflects the strong connection between the Hospice and the communities it serves. Every donation, purchase and ticket helps ensure that patients and their families continue to receive compassionate care and support when they need it most.

With another successful Summer Garden Celebration complete, attention now turns to Springhill Hospice's busy calendar of fundraising events over the coming months, as the charity continues its efforts to raise the funds needed to sustain its vital services for local people.

title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.

title: Rochdale-born TikToker investigated by Scottish police over Meta smart glasses videos
excerpt: A Rochdale-born TikTok creator known online as 'E Dobbin' is being investigated by Scottish police after complaints relating to videos recorded using Meta smart glasses.
content_html:
Scott Margerison, a Rochdale native who publishes content online under the alias 'E Dobbin', is being investigated by Scottish police following complaints about videos allegedly recorded using Meta smart glasses during a trip around Scotland.

According to the Daily Record, officers are reviewing footage to determine whether any criminal offences have been committed. The reported videos include members of the public, retail staff and CalMac employees being recorded, along with confrontational interactions and footage from the bridge of the CalMac ferry Loch Seaforth. CalMac subsequently suspended public bridge visits.

Previous controversies

The Scotland investigation is not the first controversy surrounding Margerison's online activity. He previously attracted significant public criticism after uploading footage filmed inside JD Gym in which viewers alleged he made racist and sexually explicit remarks while recording members of the public. Reports at the time indicated he was subsequently banned from the gym.

Online content

Across multiple TikTok accounts, some of which are no longer available, Margerison has published videos promoting numerous conspiracy theories and alternative historical claims. These include the Tartaria conspiracy theory, claims that the Apollo Moon landings were faked, the so-called Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory, and claims that mountains are the fossilised remains of enormous petrified creatures.

The Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory has been widely rejected by historians and researchers and is commonly associated with antisemitic conspiracy narratives.

Many of Margerison's videos challenge established historical, archaeological and scientific consensus and have generated substantial debate and criticism online.

Police investigation

Scottish police have confirmed officers received complaints and are reviewing the available material to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

At the time of publication no criminal charges have been announced. An investigation does not imply criminal guilt.
